sens: An individual of the male sex, a male
A certain person, an unspecified (identity less important than the action)
A person of consideration, a man of quality or authority
H1400.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: a man, a male individual. This is the basic word to designate a human being of the male sex, without particular detail about his age or status. In Daniel 3:21, the three companions of Daniel are called "men": this term simply states that they are people, human creatures.

2. An indefinite person, often in the plural "people" or "some." Here, the emphasis is less on the identity of the character than on his role or action. In Ezra 4:21, we speak of the "people" who were working on the reconstruction of Jerusalem — the word designates them only to refer to a group to whom an order is given, not to know them individually.

3. A man of weight, dignity, or importance: someone who matters, who has a position. In Daniel 6:5, these "men" are the king's advisors and satraps — authoritative figures who conspire against Daniel. The same word can also mean "the one who prevails," hence "to take over" in the expression "to gain the upper hand."
H1400.origine: This Aramaic word (Aramaic from Daniel and Ezra) comes from a root that means "to be strong" or "to be powerful." It is related to the Hebrew geḇer (גֶּבֶר, H1397), which also carries the idea of an adult male, a warrior, a valid and capable man. The primary meaning is that of strength and virility: a man is primarily one who has strength. In late Aramaic, the word retains this nuance, even when it simply means "someone."
H1400.emploi: This Aramaic word appears about twenty times, exclusively in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel and in the book of Ezra — the two parts of the Bible written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. Its use is very practical: it serves to designate people in decrees, court narratives, accusations. In Ezra 6:8, the elders of the Jews are "men" to whom the reconstruction costs must be paid. In Daniel 3, the three young men are "men" thrown into the furnace. In Daniel 6, the advisors who conspire against Daniel are "men" — here with a pejorative nuance. The word is often neutral, sometimes tinged with the dignity or power of those it designates.
H1400.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks first of concrete, real people, with their bodies, strengths, and weaknesses. Even in the heavens, before King Nebuchadnezzar or the advisors of King Darius, men remain vulnerable beings — but submitted to God, they can stand firm and be saved. It is a word that anchors the biblical story in reality.

sens: Who possesses great physical strength, remarkable bodily power
Who is capable of performing acts requiring exceptional strength
H1401.detail:
1. The word describes a person endowed with impressive physical strength, capable of expending great energy for tasks that require power. In Daniel 3:20, King Nebuchadnezzar orders the "strong" soldiers of his army to seize the three young men and throw them into the furnace: these are the strongest men, able to overpower prisoners and carry them to certain death.
2. More broadly, the term characterizes one who is capable, through his strength, of successfully carrying out difficult or violent actions — a robust warrior, a muscular man trained for combat or hard work.
H1401.origine: The word is from Aramaic, the language spoken by the Jews in exile in Babylon. It derives from the verb "to become strong" and belongs to the family of Hebrew *guébèr* (גֶּ֫בֶר), which means "man," "remarkable person," emphasizing the idea that a true man is recognized by his strength and authority. This root evokes the image of virile power, a capacity to act and dominate.
H1401.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel 3:20, in the account of the fiery furnace. Nebuchadnezzar asks his strongest soldiers — the most robust, the most physically capable — to capture Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and throw them into the fire. The context is that of the king's absolute power and the execution of a brutal order: the strongest men are selected for this violent task. This word emphasizes the brute strength put to the service of tyranny.
H1401.portee: This word reminds us that physical strength, even impressive, is at the service of human power — here, of an unjust power. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how the power of the world, even considerable (the strongest soldiers of the greatest empire), fails in the face of faithfulness to God: the three young men will emerge unharmed from the furnace. True strength is not muscular, but spiritual.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles who returned with Zerubbabel
H1402.detail: Gibbar is the name of a family head whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The text of Ezra 2:20 mentions him as the ancestor of a family numbering ninety-five members. The name means "the valiant one" in Hebrew, suggesting that he was a man of character and responsibility among those who rebuilt Jerusalem and its temple.
H1402.origine: The name Gibbar (גִּבָּר) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be strong" or "valiant." This root evokes the notion of power and strength. The name may also be another designation for Gibeon (the city mentioned in Ezra 2:20 in the context of the returning families), enriching the historical context of the restoration of the people after the exile.
H1402.emploi: Gibbar appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:20, in the genealogical list of families who returned from captivity in Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. He is presented as the head of a family of ninety-five people. This mention is set in the context of the reconstruction of the temple and the reorganization of the Jewish people returning to their land, showing the importance of family lineages and community continuity after deportation.
H1402.portee: This name reminds readers that the restoration of Israel after the exile was not an anonymous undertaking, but relied on courageous men and their families. It invites recognition of the role of leaders and communities in God's project, and to see in the return from exile an act of divine faithfulness toward His people.

sens: Archangel sent by God to deliver important messages
Divine messenger to the prophets and the faithful
H1403.detail:
1. Gabriel is an archangel, meaning a high-ranking angel in the celestial hierarchy. His name means "Warrior of God" or "Man of God" — he represents divine power and authority. In Daniel's vision, Gabriel presents himself to explain to the prophet the meaning of what he has seen (Daniel 8:16): he is the chosen messenger of God for major revelations.
2. Gabriel appears as the angel specialized in decisive announcements. When he manifests to Daniel a second time (Daniel 9:21), he comes during the evening prayer to communicate the prophecy of the seventy weeks — a message concerning the future of God's people. He is a trusted intermediary between heaven and earth.
H1403.origine: The name Gabriel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God is strong" or "Warrior of God" (from gâbar, "to be strong," and El, "God"). This name reflects his role: a messenger acting on behalf of divine power. In biblical and post-biblical traditions, Gabriel holds a special place among the archangels, recognized as one of the most important angels in God's service.
H1403.emploi: Gabriel is named twice in the Old Testament, only in the book of Daniel. He intervenes during the major prophetic visions of the prophet: first to explain the vision of the ram and the goat (Daniel 8:16), then to reveal the prophecy of the seventy weeks concerning the coming of the Messiah and the salvation of the people (Daniel 9:21). In both cases, he is presented as God's messenger for revelations of critical importance. His appearance is always accompanied by a decisive divine action: he comes "in swift flight" and speaks directly to the prophet with God's authority.
H1403.portee: Gabriel embodies the certainty that God communicates with His people and does not abandon them. For the reader, this archangel reminds us that God's promises are conveyed solemnly and reliably — God does not leave His servants without guidance. Gabriel's presence at critical moments in salvation history (prophetic announcements, messianic messages) ensures that God's purposes are fulfilled according to His will and timing.

sens: Woman who exercises authority or command over others
Wife of a man of high rank or power
Woman who rules or governs a people
H1404.detail: 1. The most common meaning is that of a woman who commands servants or slaves. This is the case with Sarai in Genesis: Hagar, who belongs to her as a servant, must obey her (Genesis 16:4, 16:8). The young Syrian servant speaks of her mistress with respect (2 Kings 5:3). Psalm 123:2 uses this image to describe the relationship of dependence between a servant and her mistress: just as the servant waits for the order or grace from the one who governs her, the psalmist waits for God's mercy. 2. The word can also refer to the wife of a man of high rank or power, one who shares his authority and prestige. Proverbs 30:23 evokes the explosive social tension when a servant takes the place of her mistress by marrying. 3. Rarely, the word also designates a queen or a woman who rules over a people (Isaiah 47:5, 47:7), Babylon personified as a queen who loses her throne.
H1404.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "man," "to be strong": גְּבַר (gavar). The feminine form גְּבֶרֶת (gvéret) thus designates the woman who possesses strength or authority, the feminine equivalent of master or lord (גָּבִיר, gavir). This word reflects the social structures of the ancient Near East where domestic power was exercised by the one who possessed servants.
H1404.emploi: The word appears 9 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in the narratives and poetry of the Old Testament. Three occurrences are found in the story of Hagar (Genesis 16), where Sarai is the mistress and Hagar is her fleeing servant: the word emphasizes the subordinate relationship and the dignity of the one who commands. In 2 Kings 5:3, a young Syrian captive speaks of her mistress with compassion. Psalm 123:2 uses the image to express the believer's expectation of God. Proverbs 30:23 employs it to depict a disruption of the social order. In Isaiah, the "mistress" becomes a metaphor for Queen Babylon, a symbol of earthly power destined to fall.
H1404.portee: This word helps the reader understand the structures of a biblical household and the responsibility of the one in charge. For the believer, the image from Psalm 123 — the servant who lifts her eyes to her mistress — reveals a posture of confident dependence on God: we are like servants waiting for the grace and gaze of the one who governs us. It is an invitation to humility and hope.

sens: City in the tribal territory of Dan, in Israel
Location occupied by the Philistines
Site of conflicts and sieges during the period of the kings
H1405.detail:
1. Guibbethon is a city located in the mountainous region of the territory of Dan, in the center of the country. It was initially assigned to the Levites of the family of the Kohathites, who served in the temple (Joshua 21:23), although it was surrounded by Philistine lands.
2. At the time of the reported events, the city was occupied by the Philistines, who controlled it (1 Kings 15:27). It represented a strategic point that the Israelites coveted to regain control of the region.
3. Guibbethon was the site of two successive sieges: first besieged by the troops of King Nadab of Israel (1 Kings 15:27), it also served as a rear base for Omri's armies during the campaign against Tirzah (1 Kings 16:15-17). These events mark the power struggles between the kings of Israel in the 10th century BC.
H1405.origine: The name Guibbethon literally means "mound" or "hill" in Hebrew (from the root "gib"), which describes the topography of the place. It is a city whose name reflects its geographical characteristics typical of the hilly region of Dan.
H1405.emploi: Guibbethon appears six times in the Bible, all in the historical books. It first appears as a Levitical possession assigned to the tribe of Dan during the land distribution (Joshua 19:44 and 21:23). It then becomes a major issue during the conflicts of the Northern Kingdom: it is occupied by the Philistines and besieged by the Israelites during the reign of Nadab (circa 910 BC), and later serves as a rallying point during Omri's coup against Zimri (1 Kings 15:27; 16:15-17). Its importance lies in its strategic position between the Israelite and Philistine territories.
H1405.portee: Guibbethon reminds us that ancient Israel was often contested and divided, threatened both by external enemies (the Philistines) and by internal power struggles. It symbolizes the fragility of conquered territories and the necessity for God's people to remain vigilant and united. These wartime events also show how human ambitions for power distance the kings of Israel from their mission of obedience to the covenant God.

sens: The upper surface of a house that protects from rain and sun
The high part or top of an object, especially of an altar
A place where one can go up and stay, visible from afar
H1406.detail: 1. The roof is the covering that crowns a dwelling, protecting it from the elements. It is an accessible space where life can sometimes be public. Rahab hides the spies by concealing them on the roof of her house (Joshua 2:8), a strategic and well-known location. 2. The word also refers to the top of sacred objects, notably the 'top' (roof) of the altar of incense, which Moses is to cover with pure gold (Exodus 30:3): the most visible and honored part. 3. The roof is a place where one goes up to see far, pray, or act publicly. David sees Bathsheba 'on the roof' of his house (2 Samuel 11:2), indicating that going up to the roof was a daily habit in the warm climate of the Levant.
H1406.origine: The Hebrew word gag derives from the root 'gag' which evokes the idea of what is high, emerging. It is a simple and ancient word, attested as early as Exodus. The concept reflects the architecture of the ancient Near East: houses had flat, terrace roofs that served as living spaces, storage, and circulation areas. These roofs were not steep slopes like in Northern Europe, but flat and practical surfaces.
H1406.emploi: The word 'roof' appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic narratives. It primarily refers to the roofs of ordinary houses (Joshua 2:8; 1 Samuel 9:26; 2 Samuel 11:2): places of work, prayer, or refuge. It also appears on sacred buildings and the altars of the Temple (Exodus 30:3). The prophets use it figuratively: the grass that grows on roofs and dries quickly symbolizes human fragility and the fleeting nature of the powerful (Psalms 129:6; 2 Kings 19:26). In judgment prophecies, the peoples who go up on roofs to invoke idols or seek refuge illustrate pride and waywardness (Jeremiah 19:13; Zephaniah 1:5).
H1406.portee: The roof reminds us that our lives unfold in full view of all, in broad daylight as well as under the cover of night. The house where one thinks they are hidden can be traversed, unmasked. It is also the biblical image of our fragility: like the grass on roofs that dries quickly, our human strength is short-lived. At the same time, the roof is a space for prayer and clarity — going up to the roof is lifting one's eyes to heaven.

sens: A plant whose seed is small and round
The appearance or physical resemblance of the manna to this seed
H1407.detail:
1. Coriander is an aromatic herb characterized by its small, round seeds. It is a well-known plant in cooking and perfumery in antiquity. The Bible only mentions coriander to compare manna to its seeds: 'It was like coriander seed; white' (Exodus 16:31).
2. The word here describes less the plant itself than its usefulness in describing manna. The Israelites, seeing this new food fallen from heaven each morning, compare it to what they knew: small, round, white seeds, similar to coriander seeds. This comparison appears twice to emphasize how discreet the appearance of manna was, despite its miraculous importance (Numbers 11:7).
H1407.origine: The Hebrew word גַּד (gad) designates coriander seed, whose Greek name is κόριαννον (koriannon). It comes from the coriander plant cultivated in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. The word evokes the smallness and roundness characteristic of this seed. It is not an Israeli plant: the comparison shows that the Israelites were well acquainted with the spices and herbs of the ancient world.
H1407.emploi: The word 'coriander' (gad) appears only twice in the Bible, solely in the accounts of manna in the desert. In Exodus 16:31, it describes the resemblance of manna to coriander seed to explain its appearance to the Israelites. In Numbers 11:7, the same comparison is repeated to further clarify what the people saw each day. These two occurrences serve the same purpose: to give the reader a concrete image of what manna looked like, so they understand that it was an extraordinary substance, miraculous in its origin and persistence, but recognizable by its tiny, round form.
H1407.portee: This simple comparison with coriander enriches our understanding of the miracle of manna. It reminds us that God provides in a discreet and constant manner: the miraculous food was not overwhelming or supernatural in appearance, but humble and regular. It also shows how the Israelites had to observe this small white seed each day and recognize in it divine providence. It is a lesson on daily trust in God and the recognition of His simple yet sufficient gifts.

sens: Babylonian deity of fortune and destiny
H1408.detail: Gad is the name of a foreign deity, worshiped notably in Babylon. The Bible mentions it only once, in a context of rebuke: Isaiah denounces the Israelites who 'prepare a table for Gad' (Isaiah 65:11), meaning they offer sacrifices and libations to him, abandoning the true God. These tables and filled cups are visible signs of idolatrous worship, showing how this people had turned away from the Lord to follow the gods of the surrounding nations.
H1408.origine: Gad is a proper name borrowed from the Babylonian pantheon, where it designated a tutelary deity associated with luck, fortune, and destiny. The name has no Hebrew etymology: it is a foreign term introduced into Israel by the influence of neighboring peoples.
H1408.emploi: Gad appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 65:11, where the prophet reproaches the Israelites for having prepared tables and filled cups for this Babylonian god. The context shows that this worship was part of the idolatrous practices that had seduced part of the people, particularly after contact with Babylon during the exile. The isolated mention underscores the absurdity and gravity of this abandonment: preferring a foreign god over the God who created the holy mountain and made a covenant with Israel.
H1408.portee: The mention of Gad reminds the Christian reader how idolatry takes root: not always through open rebellion, but through a gradual slide towards the beliefs of surrounding cultures. It invites us to examine our own 'prepared tables' — false hopes and modern gods — and to return to loyalty to the living God.

sens: the luck, the good fortune that befalls someone
the joy of success or prosperity
H1409.detail:
1. Happiness refers to the good luck or fortunate fate that befalls someone. It is the blessed event, unexpected or long hoped for. Leah, long barren, celebrates the arrival of her son by exclaiming, "What happiness!" — she recognizes in this birth the good hand of God granting her what she no longer dared to hope for (Genesis 30:11).
2. By extension, happiness also refers to the state of prosperity and well-being that results from this luck. It is less a personal feeling than a concrete and visible condition: to have happiness is to enjoy success, fertility, and divine protection.
H1409.origine: The Hebrew word gad comes from a root that evokes the idea of fortune or happy destiny. It is linked to the notion of luck or success that befalls someone from the outside, like a gift. The same word was used to name the tribe of Gad, son of Jacob, likely to emphasize the happy fortune of this tribe. The primary meaning remains attached to the notion of luck or favorable destiny.
H1409.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the account of the birth of Gad in Genesis 30:11. Leah, jealous of her sister Rachel and long barren, finally welcomes her seventh son. She exclaims, "Gad!" — a cry of happiness, relief, and thanksgiving to God. It is a word that springs from the heart, barely a phrase, but it captures the intensity of the moment: good fortune after waiting, joy after pain. The name given to the child perpetuates this cry of happiness.
H1409.portee: This word reminds us that true happiness, in the Bible, is not a selfish ambition but a gift from God. Leah recognizes her blessing not as the fruit of her effort, but as a divine favor. For the reader, this invites us to see life as a series of gifts awaited from God, and to welcome His blessings with gratitude and joy.

sens: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, the slave mother
Tribe of Israel descended from Gad
Prophet who served King David
H1410G.detail:
1. Gad is the seventh son of Jacob, born of Zilpah, Leah's maid. His name means "troop" or "happiness," which Leah expresses by saying, "What happiness!" at his birth (Genesis 30:11). He is the full brother of Asher and the half-brother of the other sons of Jacob.
2. The tribe of Gad descends from this son of Jacob and becomes one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It receives territory east of the Jordan, in Gilead, as reported by Moses in Numbers 32:29 when he acknowledges the sons of Gad armed for battle. This tribe is regularly mentioned in the censuses and land divisions.
3. A prophet named Gad appears during the time of King David. Although the provided roles do not mention him directly, the source indicates that he joined David in exile and intervened particularly during the punishment for the census of the people, also participating in the organization of worship.
H1410G.origine: The name Gad literally means "troop" or "happiness" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking abundance and prosperity, the idea of a numerous and happy troop. This name reflects Leah's joy at his birth. The word Gad also refers in the Old Testament to a Canaanite deity of fortune, but here it is simply a personal name carrying a blessing.
H1410G.emploi: The name Gad appears 54 times in the Old Testament, first for the son of Jacob in Genesis 30:11, and then extensively for the tribe that descends from him. The tribe of Gad is mentioned in the censuses of Numbers (1:14, 2:14, 26:15), in the division of the lands (Numbers 32, Joshua 13-14), and in events concerning it, notably its position east of the Jordan. It is also found in Moses' blessings (Deuteronomy 33:20) and in genealogical lists (1 Chronicles 2:2). Joshua 22 reports an important dialogue where the sons of Gad defend their faithfulness to the Lord. The prophet Gad is mentioned in the Davidic narratives, although indirectly here.
H1410G.portee: Gad reminds us that each tribe of Israel, even one established far from the heart of worship in Jerusalem, remains a full member of God's people. His story shows how faithfulness to the covenant is manifested in the sharing of tasks and lands, and how successive generations maintain their identity and commitment to God. The prophet Gad also illustrates the divine presence that guides kings and corrects the people in love.

sens: Prophet and advisor to King David
The son of Jacob and ancestor of a tribe of Israel
H1410H.detail:
1. Gad is a prophet who accompanies King David during his life. He first appears to David in flight in the fortress (1 Samuel 22:5), then intervenes during David's sin when he wanted to take a census of the people: Gad comes to announce the punishment and offers him the choice of judgment (2 Samuel 24:13), then conveys the order to build an altar (2 Samuel 24:18). In Chronicles, he is called "the seer of David" (1 Chronicles 21:9), which shows that he is recognized as one who sees and hears God's words on behalf of the king.
2. Gad is also the seventh son of Jacob, born of Zilpah (Leah's maid), and becomes the ancestor of the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This dual identity explains why the name appears in genealogies and why the tribe bears the same name as the prophet.
H1410H.origine: The name Gad means "troop" or "luck" in Hebrew, an image of strength and protection. This name also appears as a tribal ancestor among Jacob's twelve sons, highlighting the importance of this family in Israel's history. The prophet Gad during David's time carries this ancient name, establishing a symbolic link between the ancient history of the people and the time of David's reign.
H1410H.emploi: The prophet Gad appears 13 times in the Bible, mainly in the accounts of David (1 Samuel 22, 2 Samuel 24, 1 Chronicles 21 and 29). His role is to convey God's words to the king: he advises him to leave the fortress (1 Samuel 22:5), announces the consequences of his census sin (2 Samuel 24:13-14), tells him to build an altar (2 Samuel 24:18), and participates in the arrangements for the Temple worship (1 Chronicles 29:29, 2 Chronicles 29:25). His title of "seer" indicates that he is recognized as an interpreter of divine will to David.
H1410H.portee: Gad embodies the role of the prophet in the Davidic monarchy: one who, in full fidelity to God, speaks at the occasion of repentance and punishment, but also of restoration. His intervention during David's sin shows that no one, not even the king, is above divine law, but also that repentance opens the way to mercy. This is an important lesson on spiritual authority and the humility of power before God.

sens: Place where the Israelites camped during their desert crossing
Compound name meaning "Dibon of the tribe of Gad"
H1410I.detail:
1. Dibon-Gad is a stop on the Israelites' journey in the desert, mentioned in their itinerary between Ijjé-Abarim and Almon-Diblathaim (Numbers 33:45-46). It is a geographical site, a campsite where the people stopped during their exodus to the Promised Land.
2. The name "Dibon-Gad" combines the name of the place Dibon with the mention of the tribe of Gad, indicating that this site was in the territory occupied or controlled by this tribe. It means "the Dibon of Gad" to perhaps distinguish it from other places named Dibon.
H1410I.origine: The word "Gad" means "troop" in Hebrew and primarily refers to the son of Jacob from whom the tribe of Gad descended (Genesis 30:11). The full name "Dibon-Gad" associates the name of the place Dibon with the tribal name, thus designating the Dibon located in the land of Gad, east of the Jordan. The tribe of Gad had settled in this region of Transjordan.
H1410I.emploi: Dibon-Gad appears only twice in the Bible, in verses 45 and 46 of Numbers 33, in the complete list of the Israelites' camps in the desert. This passage systematically enumerates all the places where the people of Israel stopped during their journey from Egypt to the borders of Canaan. Dibon-Gad is listed as a stop among others, marking the progression of the exodus.

sens: Official responsible for managing the king's finances and property
Advisor or magistrate of the royal palace
H1411.detail:
1. The treasurer is a high official responsible for the administration of royal finances — he keeps, controls, and distributes the money and property of the king's treasury. In Daniel 3:2 and 3:3, he is among the officials that King Nebuchadnezzar summons to attend the dedication of the golden statue, which shows his high rank at court.
2. The term more broadly refers to a magistrate or advisor of the palace, a member of the close circle of royal dignitaries. Both usages present the treasurer alongside satraps, stewards, governors, and judges: he is a man of authority, responsible for the administration of the kingdom.
H1411.origine: The Aramaic word גְּדָֽבְרַיָּא (guédarvaïa) comes from the Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar), which itself derives from a root meaning "treasure" or "that which is hidden." The title spread in the royal courts of Mesopotamia and Persia: it was an important office, often held by a scribe or an educated man capable of managing both money and state affairs.
H1411.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Daniel (3:2 and 3:3), at the time when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar summons all the high officials and magistrates of his empire to attend the dedication of a great golden statue. These two verses enumerate the complete hierarchy of court officials: the treasurer occupies a fixed place, indicating his administrative importance and status in the organization of royal power.
H1411.portee: This word reminds us that God knows and governs all the empires of the world, including their institutions and hierarchies. Even the powerful officials of King Nebuchadnezzar are under God's control: the account in Daniel shows that their power is limited in the face of divine will.

sens: Camping site of the Israelites in the desert during the Exodus
H1412.detail: 1. Gudgoda was one of the places where the Israelites stopped during their long journey through the desert, between the exit from Egypt and the entry into the Promised Land. It is a documented stop in the itinerary of the forty years of wandering: in Deuteronomy 10:7, Moses recalls that the people passed through there on their way to Jothbath.
H1412.origine: The Hebrew name gudgodah literally means "the place of cutting" or "the place of bleeding," probably due to geographical features of the site. This same place appears elsewhere in the Bible under the name of Hor-Haggidgad (חֹר הַגִּדְגָּד), which has a similar etymology. Both names refer to the same desert stopping place.
H1412.emploi: Gudgoda appears only once in the Segond, in Deuteronomy 10:7, where Moses lists the stages of the desert journey. This passage is part of the historical reminder speech that Moses addresses to the people before their entry into the Promised Land, to revive the memory of divine mercies. This place is part of the more complete itinerary of desert encampments, also mentioned in Numbers 33.

sens: To make a cut, an incision in the skin or flesh
To voluntarily make a cut, usually on the body
To assemble, to gather in a group or crowd
H1413.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to slice or penetrate deeply, as one would with a blade. It is the action of digging, cutting, or traversing something sharply and brutally (1 Kings 18:28: the priests of Baal made cuts with swords and lances, and blood flowed on them).
2. Specifically, it denotes the act of making a voluntary cut or wound on the body. It was a pagan practice of funeral lamentation or religious ritual. God forbids it to His people in Deuteronomy 14:1: the Israelites must not make cuts for the dead, for they are children of the Lord and must distinguish themselves from others.
3. By extension, the verb can mean to assemble, to gather in a band or crowd. In Psalms 94:21 and Jeremiah 5:7, those who gather act together against the righteous or crowd into places of sin.
H1413.origine: The root גדד expresses the idea of cutting, slicing, penetrating. The primary meaning is physical: to make a clean incision. The Talmud and ancient versions indicate that the same verb can mean to gather, probably because a crowd presses together, comes closer, thickens as one cuts or digs. The Aramaic equivalent גְּדַד (gédad) has the same meaning: to cut, to slice.
H1413.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in the prophetic books and the Torah. The primary meaning (to make an incision, to cut oneself) is found in Deuteronomy 14:1, 1 Kings 18:28, Jeremiah 16:6, and Jeremiah 41:5: it is a pagan funeral or religious practice that God forbids. The secondary meaning (to assemble, to gather) appears in Psalms 94:21 and Jeremiah 5:7, often in a negative context (gathering against the righteous, pressing into sin). The usages show that the word primarily covers a physical and bodily act, then extends to collective behavior.
H1413.portee: For the believer, these passages remind us that God distinguishes His people by practices different from those of the nations: refusing to mutilate oneself is an act of obedience and faith. The prohibition of cuts also signals that God rejects rituals of physical pain to honor the dead or appease the gods—His grace is sufficient. Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible preserves the integrity of the body as a gift from God.

sens: To cut down a tree, to make it fall
To destroy, to annihilate something great
H1414.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of cutting down a tree to make it fall. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, a heavenly being commands to fell a great tree: "Cut down the tree, and chop off its branches" (Daniel 4:14). It is a concrete, physical action that involves cutting the branches and scattering the fruits.
2. Figuratively, the word expresses the idea of destruction or annihilation of a power. When the order returns in verse 23, "Cut down the tree, and destroy it," it is no longer just about cutting wood, but about symbolically destroying the greatness and strength, here represented by the majestic tree that symbolizes the king and his kingdom.
H1414.origine: This Aramaic word (the language of part of the book of Daniel) is related to the Hebrew gâdad which also means "to cut." It comes from a root expressing the action of splitting, slicing with force. The word evokes the gesture of the lumberjack who strikes the tree to make it collapse.
H1414.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Aramaic New Testament of Daniel, in verses 14 and 23 of chapter 4, in the famous vision of the Babylonian king. These two occurrences are part of the same narrative: a messenger from heaven proclaims the order to fell the symbolic tree twice. The context is eschatological and prophetic: the tree represents King Nebuchadnezzar and his reign, and the order to "fell" announces his humiliation and temporary fall before his restoration.
H1414.portee: This passage teaches that even the greatest human power remains subject to the will of God. The image of the felled tree, stripped of its majesty, reminds the believer that pride goes before a fall and that God alone holds supreme authority over all kingdoms.

sens: Edge of a watercourse, land that borders a river or stream.
Area of water overflowing its bed and covering the banks.
H1415.detail:
1. The bank is the terrestrial edge of a river or stream. It is the boundary between water and dry land. When the Jordan was at flood stage during the harvest, its waters "overflowed all its banks" (Joshua 3:15), meaning they overflowed and covered the lands that usually bordered it.
2. By extension, "bank" can also refer to the area of water that extends beyond the riverbed during a flood. When Isaiah announces that "the mighty and great waters of the river" will rise, they will spread "over all its banks" (Isaiah 8:7), encompassing both the banks and the water that temporarily submerges them.
H1415.origine: The Hebrew word גָּדָה (gadah) belongs to a family of words describing the limit or contour of something. It primarily denotes the concept of "edge" or "boundary," specifically applied to the banks that border the waters. Its meaning is concrete and geographical, rooted in the observation of rivers and streams in the Middle East, particularly the Jordan, a major watercourse in the Holy Land.
H1415.emploi: The word bank appears four times in the Old Testament, always in connection with the Jordan. It most often describes the overflowing of the river: during Israel's crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3:15 and 4:18), the river overflows its bed and submerges its banks. In 1 Chronicles 12:15, warriors cross the Jordan "when it overflowed all its banks." Isaiah 8:7 uses the image of the river overflowing its banks to symbolize the Assyrian invasion, showing how water demonstrating its natural force becomes a figure of the destructive power of an army. In all cases, "bank" emphasizes the extraordinary nature of the overflow: what is contained on its banks escapes and submerges the land.
H1415.portee: The overflowing of the Jordan is a sign of the presence and power of the Lord acting for His people (Joshua 3-4). But the image of the submerged banks also reminds us that the forces of the world, even spectacular ones, remain under God's control. For the Christian, this invites us to see in the "banks" of daily life — our limits, our boundaries — places where God manifests His strength and sovereignty.

sens: Group of warriors organized for combat
Band of raiders or soldiers on an expedition
Military division of a regular army
Attack or military incursion
H1416.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a group of fighters united for war, such as the "troops of Chaldeans" or Syrians that God sends against Judah (2 Kings 24:2): armed men forming a combat unit.
2. It can also describe an armed band, often raiders or marauders who strike and withdraw — for example, in 1 Samuel 30:8, David pursues the band that captured his family, showing that these groups loot through incursions.
3. Within a regular army, it is a subdivision, a company of soldiers counted and organized: Uzziah has "soldiers who went to war by bands" (2 Chronicles 26:11), in other words, by structured units.
4. The word can also mean the action itself, the incursion or raid: in 2 Samuel 3:22, an "excursion" is the operation being conducted.
H1416.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes cutting, division, fragmentation — the idea of sharing or dividing into parts. An armed troop is in some way a group divided into units, organized by sections. This word carries the image of a precise action: men gathering, going out together to strike, then dispersing. The same family of words expresses the idea of rupture, division, which suits warriors who break through lines or make incursions.
H1416.emploi: The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the context of war and invasion. In the Historical Books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), it describes either bands of raiders or brigands (1 Samuel 30:8), or regular military divisions (2 Chronicles 26:11), or foreign troops sent against Israel (2 Kings 24:2). In the Psalms and Job, it takes on a broader meaning: the distressed speak of "troops" of enemies surrounding them (Job 19:12; Psalms 18:30). In the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea), the word retains its sense of attack or raid, often as an instrument of divine judgment. Each usage emphasizes the organization and collective action of warriors.
H1416.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of war: it names the troops, the raids, the invasions that mark Israel's history. It also shows that even the scourges of war respond to God's plan. By reading "troops of Chaldeans" sent by the Lord, the reader understands that God masters history and governs the nations. For the believer, it is a lesson on divine sovereignty in the events of the world, even the most violent ones.

sens: ridge or groove made in the ground by the plow
relief of earth formed by the work of tillage
wound or incision made on the skin as a sign of mourning
H1417.detail:
1. A furrow is the groove or ridge made by the plow when tilling a field. The image is concrete and agricultural: God "levels the clods" of the earth (Psalms 65:11), meaning He softens and prepares the ground He has worked to produce grain.
2. The word also refers to the ridges or unevenness of soil that remain after tilling. The psalmist evokes the same divine action of watering and softening the soil to make it fertile.
3. By extension from the concrete meaning of "groove" or "cut," the word also applies to cuts or incisions that people made on their skin as a sign of mourning and deep sorrow. In Jeremiah 48:37, the Moabites in mourning make incisions on their hands, a gesture of lamentation in ancient culture.
H1417.origine: The Hebrew word גְּדוּד (geduṯ) comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to slice." It refers to an action that leaves a mark: to dig or trace a line, whether in the earth, flesh, or even stone. The primary meaning is thus that of something "cut" or "marked by a cut."
H1417.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages. First in Psalms 65:11, where it describes God's work in nature: He prepares the furrows of the field by watering and cleansing them for the harvest. Then in Jeremiah 48:37, where the context is entirely different: it concerns the ritual incisions that the Moabites make on their bodies to express their mourning and suffering. This shift in meaning — from the tilled furrow to the wound of the heart — shows how the same concrete image becomes the symbol of deep affliction.
H1417.portee: The psalm reminds us that God intervenes even in the details of the earth and its cultures. Jeremiah, on the other hand, uses this word to show the stark reality of mourning: the incisions on the body testify to a pain that only God can truly understand. For the Christian reader, these images of tillage and suffering speak of transformation and trust in divine providence.

sens: Of large size or physical dimension
Numerous or abundant in quantity
Intense or powerful in force or effect
Sonorous, resonating loudly
Aged, advanced in years
Important, of value or dignity
H1419A.detail:
1. Great primarily designates what has a considerable size or dimension: the sun is the "great" luminary, larger than the moon (Genesis 1:16); a "great" terebinth can accommodate a rider (2 Samuel 18:9).
2. The word applies to quantity: a large crowd, a "great" multitude of peoples. Abraham will become a "great" nation, meaning a people abundant in number (Genesis 12:2).
3. Great also expresses the power or intensity of an action or feeling: the "great" hand of God that performs wonders (Exodus 6:6), the "great" anger, the mourning that is "great."
4. When applied to sound, "great" means sonorous and resounding: a "great" cry, a voice that rises loudly (Psalms 108:5).
5. When speaking of people, "great" can mean older, more advanced in age: the "great" son in relation to the younger son.
6. Great also carries the sense of important, considerable in dignity or value: the "great" nations (Deuteronomy 11:23), houses of importance (Jeremiah 52:13), and particularly God the "Great" (Deuteronomy 10:17).
H1419A.origine: The Hebrew word gadol comes from the root "gâdal" which means "to grow, to increase." This root evokes the idea of growth, development: something that grows becomes larger. The same word can be used as a noun to refer to "great things" or "wonders." The family of the word includes "gadal" (to grow), "magdal" (tower, that which rises), and "godeul" (greatness). The adjective gadol thus summarizes the idea of breadth in all its aspects: size, number, power, importance.
H1419A.emploi: This word is one of the most frequently used in the Hebrew Bible (over 470 times). It appears in all historical, legislative, and poetic books, with nuances depending on the context. In Genesis, "great" first qualifies God's creations and the dimensions of the world (the stars, the creatures). It then applies to the promises made to the patriarchs: a "great" nation, a "great" offspring. In Exodus, it describes the plagues (as "great" signs) and God's mighty acts. In the historical books, it qualifies peoples, kings, warriors, and events: a victory, a defeat, a disaster can be "great." It can also express a judgment of value or an assessment of importance: a "great" man, a "great" city. Finally, "great" becomes a way to praise God Himself for His incomparable power and majesty (Deuteronomy 10:17).
H1419A.portee: The word "great" helps the reader grasp God's power and authority in creation and history. Whether it is the "great" hand of God or His "great" miracles, the word reminds us that God acts with unmatched strength. Furthermore, the use of "great" for men, nations, or events invites discernment about what truly matters: true greatness is that which God recognizes. It is not primarily physical size or military power, but faithfulness and trust in God.

sens: Man from the Exile and Return period
Father of Zabdiel, chief of the priests who returned to Jerusalem
H1419B.detail:
1. Guédolim is a man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return of Israel, at the time when the Jewish people returned from captivity in Babylon. His name literally means "the great" or "the great man" in Hebrew.

2. He is mentioned only once in the Bible as the father of Zabdiel. Zabdiel was a valiant man and chief of the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:14). The context shows that he belonged to a family of important priests.
H1419B.origine: The name Guédolim comes from the Hebrew "gadol" (גָּדוֹל) which means "great" — great in size, strength, or importance. Formed as a personal name, it designates someone who was likely respected or powerful in his community. It is simply a descriptive name of a quality or status.
H1419B.emploi: Guédolim appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:14, in the list of priests and Levites who returned to Jerusalem after the captivity in Babylon. He is presented there as the father of Zabdiel, who was a valiant man and chief of one hundred twenty-eight priests. This brief mention is part of the account of the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple worship, where the Bible lists the priestly families that participated in the return.

sens: Of large size or extent, significant in dimensions
Impressive or powerful character of a person or thing
Remarkable value, importance, or dignity
H1419J.detail:
1. This word first describes what is vast or voluminous. In the Bible, it particularly designates the great sea, meaning the Mediterranean, the natural western boundary of the promised land: "Your western boundary shall be the great sea" (Numbers 34:6). This immense sea marks the borders of Israel's territory as an impressive and insurmountable barrier.
2. The word then qualifies what is imposing, powerful, or remarkable in its extent or scope. When Joshua reminds Israel: "I have given you these nations as an inheritance, up to the great sea toward the sunset" (Joshua 23:4), he evokes the extraordinary magnitude of God's gift and the vastness of the conquered territory.
3. It can also express what is important or of great value. Although this sense is less present in the provided usages, it is implicit in the way the Bible designates the Mediterranean: it is great not only in size but also in its decisive role in the geography of the biblical world.
H1419J.origine: The Hebrew גָּדוֹל comes from a root expressing increase, growth, and extension. The same root appears in words like גָּדַל (gadal, "to grow, to increase") and גֹּדֶל (godèl, "greatness"). This word paints the image of something that extends, that increases, that occupies an important place in space or mind.
H1419J.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the provided passages, always applied to the sea (the Mediterranean) or the river (the Euphrates) as the boundary of Israel's territory. It serves to establish the geographical limits of the promised land: six usages describe the "great sea" as the western boundary (Numbers 34:6; Joshua 1:4; 15:12; 23:4; Ezekiel 47:20; 47:15). In these contexts, "great" emphasizes not only the actual size of this sea but also its theological role: it materializes the boundaries that God has set for His people. The adjective highlights the magnitude of the divine gift and the precise limits of an inheritance.
H1419J.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God establishes clear boundaries and knows perfectly the extent of what He offers to His people. The "great" sea is not a chaotic threat, but a fixed boundary in God's plan. This encourages trust: God knows how to measure His gifts and delineates a specific territory for His people's inheritance, demonstrating both His generosity and wisdom.

sens: Of large size or dimension
In high number
Of marked intensity or force
Loud, noisy
Older, elder
Of major importance, illustrious
H1419K.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what has a large physical extent or dimension: a great city, a bulky object. This is the simplest and most concrete image.

2. It applies to what is numerous, abundant in quantity: a great multitude, a great army. "The hand of the Lord was against the city, and there was a very great panic" (1 Samuel 5:9) — the panic is vast, seizing all the inhabitants.

3. It qualifies what possesses great strength, great intensity: great sorrow, great fear. The adjective then measures the power of an emotion or action.

4. It describes what produces a great noise, what is loud or resounding: a great voice, a great cry.

5. It designates one who is older compared to others in a sibling group: the elder. Japheth is said to be "the brother of Japheth the elder" (Genesis 10:21), Esau is the "firstborn son" (Genesis 27:15), Leah is "the elder" of Laban's two daughters (Genesis 29:16). This sense appears most frequently in the biblical usages provided.

6. It qualifies one who possesses great importance, great authority, or who is renowned and distinguished: a great man, a great figure. The word can even refer to God Himself in His absolute greatness.
H1419K.origine: The Hebrew word גָּדוֹל comes from a primitive root expressing the idea of growth and extension. It belongs to a family that also includes "to grow" and "greatness." The word is fundamental in biblical Hebrew: it paints the image of what extends, enlarges, rises. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it often corresponds to the Greek megas (μέγας), which carries the same idea.
H1419K.emploi: This word is very frequent in the Old Testament. Among the fifteen usages noted here, the majority place it in genealogical or familial contexts: David is the youngest, while his three elders (1 Samuel 17:14) followed Saul, or Saul offers David his eldest daughter Merab in marriage (1 Samuel 18:17). The word also applies to age differences among children. Outside of this context of relative age, it retains its meaning of "great" in intensity or extent: the great panic that falls upon the city of Gath (1 Samuel 5:9) shows how the adjective measures the amplitude of a reality. The word can qualify cities, things, or people: one can be great by age (elder), by rank (great man), or by importance.
H1419K.portee: This word teaches that greatness, whether of age, size, or importance, is a common biblical category for organizing realities. Understanding who is the elder, who is great, who has authority, is to grasp the order of families and communities as the Bible perceives it. It is also to recognize that in the divine plan, the order of births and the status of individuals are never neutral: God causes children to be born in a precise order, and this order has significance.

sens: characteristic of what is great, immense, or imposing
magnificence, splendor
remarkable act or work, miracles
H1420.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the quality of what is great, vast, impressive in size or importance. In 1 Chronicles 29:11, we speak of "the greatness" of the Lord alongside His strength and magnificence: it is the incomprehensible vastness of God.
2. It also expresses a kind of visible magnificence, a splendor that can be contemplated. Esther 1:4 describes how the king "showed the splendid wealth of his kingdom and the dazzling magnificence of his greatness": it is the pomp, the brilliance of a royal court.
3. Finally, the word can designate grand acts, miracles, impressive works that only God can accomplish. In 2 Samuel 7:23 and 1 Chronicles 17:21, we speak of the "miracles and wonders" He performed for Israel: His "great things" that testify to His power.
H1420.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be great" or "to grow great." It is a feminine noun that expresses a quality, a nature, a state. The Bible uses it mainly to speak of the greatness of God, a quality that summarizes all His perfections: His immensity, His power, His magnificence.
H1420.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Psalms and in historical books. David uses it when speaking to God (2 Samuel 7:21; 1 Chronicles 17:19) to praise the "great things" that the Lord has accomplished for him and for Israel. The Psalms often speak of the transcendent greatness of God, which surpasses all limits (Psalms 145:3 and 145:6). The book of Esther uses it to describe earthly splendor, the magnificence of the royal palace. It is a major word to express both divine majesty and the wonders it produces.
H1420.portee: This word helps us perceive the greatness of God, not as an abstraction, but as a reality that manifests concretely: through His powerful acts, through the beauty and order of His creation, through His majesty that makes hearts tremble. Understanding the greatness of God also means recognizing that His promises never fail and that His power extends to all that exists. It is an invitation to worship.

sens: insulting words, slurs directed at someone
serious offense to dignity, honor
public contempt, humiliation
H1421.detail:
1. The word designates harsh and hurtful words, insults hurled against a person or people. In Zephaniah 2:8, Moab and the Ammonites direct "outrages" at the people of Israel: these are words of mockery and contempt.
2. Outrage is an offense that seriously affects the dignity and honor of the one who receives it. In Isaiah 43:28, God declares that He has treated the leaders of the sanctuary "as profane" and delivered Israel to "outrages," meaning to humiliation and public shame.
3. It is a contempt manifested openly, often accompanied by arrogance. The outrages of the enemy nations of Israel expressed not only insults but also a pretension to dominate: Moab and Ammon "arose with arrogance against its borders."
H1421.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to outrage, insult, blaspheme." It is close to terms that express dishonor and profanation. The biblical context shows that to outrage is to treat someone without respect, to publicly belittle them, to strip them of their honor.
H1421.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the plural ("outrages"), in prophetic writings. In Isaiah 43:28, it designates the shame inflicted on Israel as a consequence of divine judgment. In Isaiah 51:7, the prophet exhorts the people not to fear the outrages of men, showing that they are merely human contempt in the face of God's promises. In Zephaniah 2:8, it refers to the arrogant words of neighboring nations, enemies of Israel. The word always expresses a serious, public insult, mixed with disdain.
H1421.portee: This word reminds us that the contempt and insults of men should not make us tremble: God alone gives true dignity and honor to His people. In the face of the world's outrages, the believer can find in God an unshakable security, for the opinion of men passes, while the love and protection of God remain.

sens: Insulting word, mockery directed at someone
State of dishonor and public humiliation
H1422.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a word that hurts: a mockery, an insult, a taunt directed at someone to belittle and ridicule them. It is the crude word of one who mocks.
2. By extension, it is the state of humiliation and dishonor that results: the target becomes an object of contempt for others. In Ezekiel 5:15, Jerusalem, struck by God's judgments, will not only be offended by words: it will become a living shame, a spectacle of ruin in the eyes of neighboring nations, and its destruction will be both an insult to its past pride and a terrifying lesson for those who see it.
H1422.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to break" or "to crush": the basic image is that of a word that breaks, that destroys reputation. Shame is what remains when dignity has been shattered. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, used to denote not only the insult uttered but the public humiliation that follows.
H1422.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 5:15. The prophet uses it to announce to Jerusalem that its ruins will become a shame among the nations: it will be looked upon with contempt, serve as a warning to neighboring peoples, and embody the humiliation caused by God's judgments. It is an act of divine word that transforms a capital into an object of mockery.
H1422.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment has a public scope: it is not a hidden matter, but a manifest shame that all can see. For the believer, it invites a serious consideration of the divine word and not to provoke, through rebellion, a fall that would become a spectacle of humiliation. It is also a call to reverence toward God rather than confidence in one's own strength.

sens: Young of the goat, domestic animal of the flock
Meat of kid used in food and sacrifices
Animal offered in sacrifice to God
H1423.detail:
1. The kid is the young male of the goat, raised in the flocks of biblical families as a domestic animal. It is an easy animal to raise, useful for wool, milk, and meat. It is easily recognized: Manoah offers a kid in sacrifice to the Lord on a rock (Judges 13:19), showing that it was a valuable and esteemed animal.
2. The meat of kid is a prized dish, regularly consumed: Rebekah asks Jacob to go get her "two good kids" to make a savory dish for her father Isaac (Genesis 27:9). Gideon also, to honor the Lord, "prepares a kid" and makes it a sacrifice (Judges 6:19).
3. The kid is an animal offered in sacrifice to God and thus has religious significance. It is a valuable item that can be given as a pledge (Genesis 38:17). The Lord forbids to "boil a kid in its mother's milk" (Exodus 34:26), showing that this rite was practiced among neighboring peoples and that Israel was to abstain from it.
H1423.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "shoot" or "young one." It is a natural diminutive: one speaks of the young of the goat as one would speak of a young shoot. The kid is an animal that appears regularly in the family and cultic narratives of the Old Testament, as goat herding was an important part of the economy and diet of Hebrew clans.
H1423.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Genesis and Judges. It designates either the living animal from the flock (Genesis 27:9, 38:17), the animal to be prepared for cooking (Judges 6:19), or the sacrificial offering. Kids are mentioned in significant moments: the story of Judah and Tamar, where a kid serves as a pledge (Genesis 38), or Gideon's calling by the Lord, which he celebrates by preparing a kid. The prohibition in Exodus 34:26 shows that the kid also had a place in the cultic practices of Canaanite peoples, which the Israelite Law condemned.
H1423.portee: For the believer, the kid reminds us that God values the simple and domestic goods of the humble. These animals from modest flocks become the means by which honor is offered to God (Judges 13:19) or a promise is sealed (Genesis 38:17). It is also a sign of the daily closeness between the shepherd's life and his communion with the Lord: by offering the fruit of his flock, one gives of oneself.

sens: father of King Menahem of Israel
H1424.detail: Gadi is a man from the kingdom of Israel during the time of the division between Israel and Judah. He is known as the father of Menahem, who became king of Israel. Menahem rose from Tirzah to Samaria, killed Shallum, and took power in his place (2 Kings 15:14), then reigned for ten years over Israel (2 Kings 15:17). Gadi himself appears only through the genealogy of his son in these two passages.
H1424.origine: The name Gadi means "my fortune" in Hebrew. It comes from a Hebrew root evoking wealth or what is granted, which was a wish for blessing for a newborn child. This type of personal name was common in ancient Israel.
H1424.emploi: Gadi appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in the account of 2 Kings 15. He is mentioned as the father of King Menahem, who reigned over the northern kingdom (Israel) in the thirty-ninth year of King Azariah of Judah. These two verses aim to establish the genealogy and identity of the king who had just taken power by violence.

sens: son of Jacob and Zilpah, ancestor of the tribe of Israel that bears his name
member of the tribe of Gad
people or region associated with the tribe of Gad
H1425.detail:
1. Gad is one of the twelve sons of Jacob. His mother is Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. He is born according to Genesis 30:11, and his name means "good fortune" or "happiness." His brothers and half-brothers are Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin, as well as his sister Dinah.
2. The Gadites are the descendants of Gad, forming one of the twelve tribes of Israel. They receive territory in Transjordan (east of the Jordan), notably in Gilead. Deuteronomy 3:16 specifies: "To the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave a part of Gilead." 
3. The word "Gad" also refers to the territory inhabited by this tribe, often mentioned alongside Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh, who shared the lands from Aroer to Bashan (2 Kings 10:33).
H1425.origine: The name Gad means "good fortune" or "luck" in Hebrew. According to Genesis 30:11, Leah would have given this name to her son saying, "What luck!" The term designates both the historical person and the community that descends from him. The tribe of Gad is well attested throughout the history of Israel, from the desert to the division of the kingdom.
H1425.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the French Old Testament, mainly in the books of Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Kings, and Chronicles. It designates sometimes the son of Jacob (Genesis 30:11), sometimes the tribe of Gad, sometimes the Gadites (descendants or warriors). The Gadites receive their inheritance in Transjordan (Numbers 34:14; Joshua 1:12; Joshua 13:8). Moses gives them the land of Gilead, from the Arnon to the Jabbok (Deuteronomy 3:16). They participate in the wars of Israel and are mentioned during the conquest of Canaan. In 2 Kings 10:33, the land of the Gadites is struck by the king of Syria. The tribe is also famous for its warriors, notably Jahzeel son of Hotham (2 Samuel 23:36) and other heroes listed in Chronicles.

sens: son of Susi, spy sent by Moses
H1426.detail: Gaddi is a man chosen by Moses to be one of the twelve spies sent to scout the land of Canaan. He represents the tribe of Manasseh, one of the northern tribes descended from Joseph. Nothing else is known about him other than this unique mission reported in Numbers 13:11.
H1426.origine: The name Gaddi means "my fortune" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing the idea of happiness or luck. It is a meaningful name, common among the Hebrews, that expresses a blessing or divine favor.
H1426.emploi: Gaddi appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:11, where he is named as one of the twelve spies. Moses had sent a representative from each of the twelve tribes to explore Canaan before the people's entry. Gaddi represented Manasseh, which was an important tribe as it descended from Joseph. No details are given about his role in the spying mission or his report upon return.

sens: Man of the Exodus and desert period
One of the twelve spies sent to scout Canaan
Representative of the tribe of Zebulun
H1427.detail:
1. Gaddiel is a man who lived during the time of the Exodus, during the crossing of the desert with Israel. His name means "God is my fortune" — it is a name that expresses trust in God for prosperity.

2. Moses appointed him as one of the twelve spies tasked with scouting the land of Canaan before the people entered it. Gaddiel represented his tribe, Zebulun, in this mission (Numbers 13:10). He was among the explorers who saw the cities, the crops, and the inhabitants of this promised land.

3. Although Gaddiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, his name is listed among those of the twelve explorers who reported their observations to Moses and the community of Israel, a decisive moment for the faith of the people.
H1427.origine: The name Gaddiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Gad" (fortune, luck) and "El" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning that God is the last element, a common formula in Israelite names to express that a reality — here fortune — comes from God. Gaddiel's father was named Sodi.
H1427.emploi: Gaddiel appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:10, where he is named among the twelve spies that Moses sends to scout Canaan. He is presented as the representative of the tribe of Zebulun, son of Sodi. This spying mission is a crucial moment in the Exodus narrative: the twelve explorers must examine the territory, its resources, and its inhabitants, and then report their observations to Moses and the assembled people.
H1427.portee: Gaddiel reminds us that every believer, no matter how discreetly they act, has their place in God's plan. Although his story is not developed in the Bible, his presence among the twelve spies shows that God sees and counts each of those who serve Him, even those whose names are not remembered by posterity.

sens: Young goat, particularly female
Livestock in ancient Israel
Poetic image of grace and beauty
H1429.detail:
1. A kid is a young animal from the goat family, particularly a female. It is a small, agile, and graceful creature.
2. In ancient Israel, goats and their young were commonly raised for their milk, meat, and hides. They were a valuable asset for shepherds and family herds.
3. In the Song of Songs (1:8), kids are used as a poetic image: the beloved is advised to graze her kids "near the dwellings of the shepherds," meaning to stay close to those who love her. The kid evokes delicacy and beauty, qualities that the poem associates with the one who is loved.
H1429.origine: The Hebrew word גְּדִיָּה (gédiyya) specifically refers to the young female animal. It comes from a root that denotes the goat and its offspring. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the kid appears mainly in pastoral and sacrificial contexts. It is a humble and familiar animal, well-known throughout Israel.
H1429.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Songs 1:8. There, the friends of the beloved advise her to graze her kids near the shepherds — an image that reinforces the idea of intimacy, affectionate care, and simple rural life. The unique usage of the word emphasizes its poetic role in this love song.
H1429.portee: The kid reminds us that the Bible uses simple and everyday realities of rural life to express the deepest feelings: love, tenderness, beauty. This image of the young animal entrusted to affectionate care speaks to the reader about the bond between the lover and the beloved.

sens: Bundle of cut and tied grains
Harvest in general, what is gathered from the field
Complete existence, life lived to its end
H1430A.detail:
1. A sheaf is a bundle of stalks of wheat or another grain, cut at harvest and tied together. It is the basic unit of fieldwork: one cuts, ties, and forms sheaves to facilitate transport and storage. Exodus 22:6 refers to sheaves as material goods that can be damaged by fire.
2. The word can more broadly refer to the harvest itself, everything that is cut and gathered. In Judges 15:5, Samson sets fire to the Philistines' sheaves: this is a destruction of their entire harvest, a very serious loss.
3. The word takes on a figurative meaning: a life lived to its end and harvested at the right time. In Job 5:26, the text compares a long and fulfilling life to a sheaf gathered in its time, meaning an existence that has reached its natural fullness and concludes at the time appointed by God.
H1430A.origine: The Hebrew word גָּדִישׁ (gadish) literally means what is piled or accumulated. Its root evokes the image of a heap or mound. It is found in agricultural contexts: it is the fruit of the labor of the reaper, what accumulates when one cuts and gathers the ears of grain.
H1430A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 22:6, it refers to a law: if a fire destroys sheaves, the responsible party must compensate. In Judges 15:5, it is an act of war: the sheaves become the object of Samson's vengeance against the Philistines. In Job 5:26, the context is that of divine promise: a long and complete life is compared to a sheaf gathered at the right moment. The word remains attached to the concrete image of agricultural work, even when it takes on a spiritual significance.
H1430A.portee: For the reader, the sheaf reminds us that life has a natural cycle: sowing, growth, harvest, gathering. It speaks of fulfillment: a life "like a sheaf in its time" means having lived long and well, arriving at the end at the appointed time. It is an image of blessing and fullness that invites everyone to seek a useful and completed life, guided by God.

sens: grave dug in the earth or rock
place where the body of a dead person rests
H1430B.detail:
1. A tomb is a pit or cavity dug in the earth or rock to bury a dead person. It is the final resting place of the human body, distinct from a simple burial. In Job 21:32, the text speaks of someone who "still watches over his tomb," suggesting a burial in the earth, durable and recognizable.
2. By extension, the tomb also refers to the burial place or the funerary monument itself, the place where one remembers the dead. It is less about the act of burying than about the permanent resting place.
H1430B.origine: The Hebrew word גָּדִישׁ (gadish) comes from a root that evokes the idea of excavation or heap: to dig and pile up the earth. It is related to terms that denote a mound, a hill, or a pile of earth. In the Hebrew Bible, tombs were often individual pits or caves, marked by a visible mound so that travelers would respect and not profane it.
H1430B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond: in Job 21:32, in a passage where Job describes the fate of the wicked. Even after death, this wicked person "is carried to a sepulcher" — literally, his tomb still receives honor and "one watches over his tomb." This unique usage shows that the word evokes funerary dignity, the attention given to the burial place of a man, good or bad.
H1430B.portee: This mention of the tomb reminds us that death is the common end for all men, and that even the wicked receive a burial. For the believer, the tomb is not the end: resurrection transforms the meaning of death. This simple word invites reflection on what remains after us and on the hope beyond the grave.

sens: Physically grow, become an adult
Increase in number, strength, or importance
Be raised, nourished, trained
Be magnified, exalted, praised
Manifest one's greatness, power
H1431.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: a child grows and becomes an adult. Isaiah 1:2 says, "I have nourished and brought up children," while Genesis 21:8 reads, "the child grew" (Isaac). This is the natural growth of a person.

2. The word also expresses increase in number, wealth, or importance. In Genesis 26:13, Abraham "became very great" in flocks and servants: this is the growth of a power.

3. To be raised means to care for a child, to nourish and train them. In 2 Kings 10:6, the kings "raised" the sons of the king at court: this is receiving an education.

4. The word also expresses exaltation or praise: "Exalt the Lord with me!" (Psalms 34:4). This is celebrating someone's greatness, publicly glorifying them.

5. Finally, it designates God manifesting His power and holiness. Ezekiel 38:23 announces, "I will manifest My greatness and My holiness" — God will make Himself known through His glorious works.
H1431.origine: The Hebrew root gadal evokes the image of expansion, of something that stretches and grows. It is related to the idea of becoming wide, spacious, large in scope. The word appears in several forms in Hebrew: the simple (to grow), the causative (to cause to grow), and the reflexive (to magnify oneself). It is a foundational word to express growth and greatness in all areas of life.
H1431.emploi: This verb has 114 occurrences in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used to describe the childhood and growth of people — Samson, Samuel, David growing under God's watch. It also applies to the increase of wealth and power: Abraham, David, Solomon become greater and greater. A frequent usage is in education and upbringing: to nourish and raise children or animals. In the Psalms and prophetic narratives, it takes on a spiritual dimension: to exalt and magnify the Lord, to acknowledge His unmatched power (Psalms 34:4, Ezekiel 38:23). The context shows that the word remains concrete, rooted in human experience: we grow, we raise, we praise — but always with the awareness that it is the Lord who gives growth.
H1431.portee: This word teaches the believer that growth — spiritual, moral, in faith — is natural and desired. To grow in the fear of God means to be nourished by His word and love. The verb also invites recognition and magnification of the Lord's greatness in one's life: it is not an act of flatness, but an honest expression of who He is. Finally, for a parent or educator, the word reminds of the responsibility to raise a generation in the knowledge and obedience to God.

sens: Become larger in size or physical strength
Increase in number, wealth, or power
Grow in importance, prestige, or influence
Be strong, robust, vigorous
H1432.detail: 1. To grow primarily means to become larger physically: the young Samuel "continued to grow" (1 Samuel 2:26), a simple image of childhood blossoming. 2. The word is also used to express increase in wealth or quantity: Isaac "grew richer and richer" (Genesis 26:13), his flocks and goods multiplying endlessly. 3. To grow can mean to rise in power and prestige: King Jehoshaphat "grew to the highest degree of greatness" (2 Chronicles 17:12), strengthening his reign through fortresses. 4. The word also describes the strength or vigor of a person: Ezekiel speaks of the Egyptians as having "strong bodies" (Ezekiel 16:26), evoking their physical power.
H1432.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of becoming great, of increasing. It is related to the name גָּדוֹל (great) and other words in the same family meaning greatness. The basic image is that of natural growth: like a plant that grows, a child that matures, a wealth that accumulates.
H1432.emploi: The verb grow appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used for the physical growth of a young person (Samuel), for the increase of wealth and goods (Isaac), for the elevation in power and prestige of a king (Jehoshaphat), and to describe the physical strength of warriors (Egyptians). In each context, the word emphasizes an observable and often impressive increase: the young person grows well, the man continually grows rich, the king asserts himself more, the body is powerful.
H1432.portee: This word reminds the reader that growth — whether physical, spiritual, or material — is a biblical reality. It also speaks of the divine blessing that allows the recipient to strengthen and prosper. To see growth or enrichment can be a mark of grace, as with Samuel who "was pleasing to the Lord": but the text also invites discernment as to whether this growth serves good or diverts from the path of God.

sens: Character of what is great, vast, imposing
Power, striking and visible strength
Magnificence, divine or royal splendor
Glory, honor, fame
Pride, arrogance, haughtiness (in a negative sense)
H1433.detail:
1. The word first designates the dimension, the extent of something: "What god is there, in heaven or on earth, who can do according to your works and your mighty acts?" (Deuteronomy 3:24). This is greatness as an observable, measurable fact.
2. It then expresses impressive power, especially divine power: "You have shown Your servant Your greatness and Your mighty hand" (Deuteronomy 3:24). This is power in action, manifest.
3. It designates magnificence or splendor in all its richness: Moses calls Israel to recognize the mighty acts of the Lord, His greatness and His strong hand (Deuteronomy 11:2). This is the visible brilliance and majesty.
4. The word approaches "glory": "Give glory to our God!" (Deuteronomy 32:3) expresses the honor due to God for who He is and what He does.
5. In a negative sense, it can denote human arrogance and pride: Isaiah denounces "the pride of the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 10:12), the pride that swells against God.
H1433.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to be great," "to grow." It designates the state or quality of what is great. In Hebrew, the same root produces the adjective "great" and the verb "to grow." The word emphasizes the concrete extent and the impression of power it provokes.
H1433.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the context of praise to God. In the Pentateuch (Numbers and Deuteronomy), it designates divine greatness and power, manifested in miracles and covenants: we ask God to forgive according to His greatness of mercy (Numbers 14:19), or we celebrate the greatness He showed in delivering Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 9:26). The Psalms use it to express praise: "celebrate His greatness" (Psalms 150:2). In the prophets, especially Isaiah and Ezekiel, the word also describes human pride, that of the king of Assyria or the Pharaoh of Egypt, who oppose the true greatness of God. Thus, the same word, depending on the context, either celebrates or denounces.
H1433.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the extent and splendor of God, to give Him the honor He deserves, and to measure their own smallness before Him. It also reminds that all human greatness that rises against God is vanity and pride. Understanding this divine greatness strengthens trust in His power and mercy.

sens: Braided cord or tassel attached to the corner of a garment
Decorative network or chain on an architectural structure
H1434.detail:
1. A fringe is a cord or a set of braided threads that are attached to the corners of a garment, particularly at the four corners of a cloak or robe. In Deuteronomy 22:12, God commands Israel to put fringes on the four corners of their garments: it serves as a visible sign, a concrete reminder of obedience to the Law.
2. The same word also refers to an architectural decoration: festoons or networks shaped in chains, placed on the capitals of the temple columns. In 1 Kings 7:17, the foreman Hiram creates these ornamental elements to adorn the tops of the bronze pillars, giving the structure an elaborate elegance.
H1434.origine: The Hebrew word גְּדִלִים (gedilim) comes from the root גדל (gadal), which means "to grow" or "to be great." The idea is of something that stretches or develops, hence the meaning of "braided cord" or "elongated ornament." The fringe is a small visible element that hangs, that unfolds — a detail that stands out.
H1434.emploi: The word gedilim appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. First, in Deuteronomy 22:12, in a cultic and moral ordinance: the fringes on the garment serve as a reminder of the Law.
