Secondly, in 1 Kings 7:17, in the description of the ornaments of the temple built by Solomon: the network festoons on the bronze columns testify to the luxury and finesse of the priestly work. In both cases, the word evokes a visible decoration, attached to what is important — the garment of the believer or the building of worship.
H1434.portee: For the Christian reader, the fringe in Deuteronomy serves as a reminder that faith must be visible and tangible, an outward sign that anchors the memory of God. The fringe is not a vain ornament, but a permanent reminder. In the context of the temple, the decoration shows that beauty and order are fitting for authentic worship: God loves the finesse of execution and the nobility of the place where He is prayed to.

sens: Leader of a family of temple slaves who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Leader of the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H1435G.detail:
1. Guiddel is the leader of the first family mentioned: the sons of Guiddel, temple slaves, who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel to rebuild Jerusalem (Ezra 2:47). This was a group of workers dedicated to the service of the sanctuary.
2. Guiddel is also the leader of a second family, that of the descendants of the servants of King Solomon, who also participated in the return from exile (Nehemiah 7:49). These two families bore the same name and both held positions of service in the temple.
H1435G.origine: The name Guiddel comes from Hebrew and literally means "very great" or "magnificent." It is a compound name expressing greatness. Although the name is held by two leaders of different families, it is likely a title or a family name passed down among the temple servants.
H1435G.emploi: Guiddel appears twice in the Bible, both times in the lists of exiles who returned to Jerusalem: once in the book of Ezra and once in the book of Nehemiah. These two parallel passages enumerate the families of temple slaves and the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned to Judah after the Babylonian captivity. Guiddel designates the family leader whose descendants bore his name and continued to serve in the rebuilt temple.

sens: Name of a family leader of temple servants during the time of exile and return
H1435H.detail: Guiddel is the name of a family leader among the temple servants who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel during the restoration of Jerusalem. His name appears in the lists of families of sacred servants (Ezra 2:56 and Nehemiah 7:58), always mentioned alongside the sons of Jaala and the sons of Darkon. These temple servants formed a category lower than that of the Levites but played an important role in the religious services of the restored temple.
H1435H.origine: The name Guiddel comes from Hebrew and literally means "very great" or "made great." It expresses greatness or excellence, a common theme in Hebrew names of the time. It is a proper name, not a title: it designates a specific person whose descendants formed a well-identified family among the people of God returned from captivity.
H1435H.emploi: Guiddel is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in the context of the return from exile: in Ezra 2:56 and Nehemiah 7:58. These two passages are practically identical: they list the leaders of the families of temple servants who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. Guiddel represents an entire family of these servants, of which only the family leader is named. His appearance in these two lists shows the administrative importance of this family at the time of the temple's reconstruction.

sens: priest during the time of Ezra
H1436A.detail: Gedaliah is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile. He is listed among the sons of Joshua, son of Jozadak, the high priest, and he had married a foreign woman — which was forbidden by the law of Moses. Ezra 10:18 names him among those who had to repudiate their foreign wives to conform to the Law and the purity of the restored people.
H1436A.origine: The name Gedaliah comes from Hebrew and means "Jehovah is great" or "The Lord is my greatness." It is a theophoric name, formed with the divine name. The name is borne by three different men in Scripture, but this one is distinguished by his role: an ordinary priest of the temple, son of the high priest, during the time of reconstruction after the Babylonian exile.
H1436A.emploi: Gedaliah appears only once in the canonical Bible, in Ezra 10:18. He lived during the time of Ezra and the return from exile, that is, in the 5th century B.C., after the destruction of the temple and the captivity in Babylon. Like many Jews who returned to the Holy Land, he had contracted a mixed marriage with a foreign woman — probably a Babylonian or a woman from a Levantine people. Ezra gathered the religious authorities and urged them to send away these wives to preserve cultic purity and the identity of the people. Gedaliah, despite his status as a priest and a member of a prestigious priestly family, had to submit to this order.

sens: governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
son of Ahikam, himself the son of Shaphan
trusted man of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar
H1436B.detail: Gedaliah is the name of a man who governed Judah after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. Nebuchadnezzar appointed him to lead the people who remained in the land (2 Kings 25:22), as a representative of Babylonian authority. Gedaliah was the son of Ahikam, an influential officer in the royal court, which explains his appointment to this position of trust. He sought to reassure the refugees and surviving warriors, swearing to them that they could live in peace if they served the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 40:9). However, his conciliatory policy could not prevent the tragedy: Ishmael, a member of the royal family, fatally struck him in the seventh month, ending his government and plunging the survivors back into chaos (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1-3).
H1436B.origine: His name means "Yahweh is great" (from the Hebrew gedôl, "great," and Yah, an abbreviation of God's name). This name expresses confidence in divine greatness, even in the midst of Babylonian captivity. Three men bore this name in Israel's history: a son of Jeduthun during the time of King David, this governor of Judah, and a son of the priest Pashhur during the time of the prophet Jeremiah.
H1436B.emploi: Gedaliah appears 22 times in the Bible, mainly in the parallel accounts of 2 Kings 25 and the book of Jeremiah (chapters 40-41). In 2 Kings 25:22, Nebuchadnezzar appoints him governor over the remnant of the people. Jeremiah 40 shows him welcoming the surviving warriors and reassuring them about the possibility of a peaceful life under Babylonian rule. Jeremiah 41 reports his assassination by Ishmael and his accomplices, an event that marked a tragic turning point for the survivors of Judah. The account highlights both his administrative goodwill and the political instability that persisted after the destruction of Jerusalem.
H1436B.portee: The story of Gedaliah illustrates how, even after God's judgment on Jerusalem, He left a path of hope and reconstruction for His people. The choice of a just governor, capable of listening and seeking peace, shows that God did not completely close His door. His assassination, though painful, also reveals the fragility of human arrangements without a foundation in God. Gedaliah's life reminds us that faithfulness to God does not guarantee earthly security, but nonetheless opens a path toward restoration and divine mercy.

sens: governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem
son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan
trusted man of the king of Babylon
H1436G.detail: Gedaliah is a figure from the time of the fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.). The king of Babylon appointed him governor over the remaining cities of Judah (Jeremiah 40:5). He is the son of Ahikam, himself the son of Shaphan, an influential family in the Kingdom of Judah that often opposed the destruction of Jeremiah. Gedaliah thus represents the political authority that the Babylonians established to administer the conquered lands. Several surviving Jewish military leaders, including Johanan and Ishmael, gathered around him at Mizpah (Jeremiah 40:8). Tragically, Ishmael kills him shortly thereafter, leading to a new crisis and the forced departure of the rest of the population (Jeremiah 41:16).
H1436G.origine: The name means in Hebrew "Jehovah is great." It is composed of "Gedol" (greatness) and the divine name "Yah." It is a classic theophoric name in ancient Judah, expressing confidence in the greatness of God. The historical figure of Gedaliah is well known in Jewish tradition as a transitional figure after the exile, even though his governorship was brief and tragic.
H1436G.emploi: Gedaliah appears four times in the book of Jeremiah (40:5, 40:6, 40:8, 41:16), all occurrences taking place during the fall of Jerusalem and its immediate aftermath. These verses show him first established by the king of Babylon as governor of the cities of Judah (40:5). Jeremiah himself comes to join him at Mizpah (40:6). Several surviving military officers then rally to him (40:8). Finally, Ishmael son of Nethania treacherously kills him, and Johanan gathers the rest of the population to save them from the hands of the murderer (41:16).
H1436G.portee: Gedaliah embodies the political fate of Judah after the destruction: a just and capable man, but whose authority remains fragile and ultimately broken by internal rivalries. His assassination shows that even the survivors of the siege do not find peace. For the believer, this account reminds us how God allowed for a partial restoration under foreign domination, and how political faithfulness is never guaranteed without divine grace.

sens: Man from the time of the Divided Monarchy, ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah
H1436H.detail: Gedaliah is a man's name that appears in the genealogy of the prophet Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1). He is the father of Cushai and the son of Amariah. His name means "the Eternal is great" in Hebrew, expressing the greatness and power of God.
H1436H.origine: The name Gedaliah is composed of two Hebrew elements: "gedol" (great) and "Yah" (the Eternal). He belonged to a family of some social importance, as his descendants include a prophet recognized by God. This type of theophoric name (containing the divine name) was common in Israel to express a confession of faith in the greatness of the God of Israel.
H1436H.emploi: Gedaliah is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Zephaniah 1:1, where he appears in the genealogy of the prophet Zephaniah. The context shows that he lived before the reign of Josiah (639-609 B.C.), during the period of the Divided Monarchy in Israel and Judah. His inclusion in this official genealogy indicates that he belonged to a respected lineage, although we do not know any details about his personal life or actions.

sens: Levitical musician during the time of David, son of Jeduthun
H1436I.detail: 1. Gedaliah was a son of Jeduthun, himself a musician and prophet during the time of King David. He appears in the list of temple singers that David organized for liturgical service (1 Chronicles 25:3). Gedaliah and his brothers formed a group of twelve musicians who were assigned a portion of the temple service, drawn by lot as indicated in 1 Chronicles 25:9: "The first lot fell to Asaph, to Joseph; the second, to Gedaliah, he, his brothers, and his sons, twelve."
H1436I.origine: The name Gedaliah means "the Eternal is great" (from "Godel" = greatness, and "Yah" = Eternal). It is a theophoric name, meaning it proclaims the greatness of God, which was common among the Levites responsible for praising the Eternal. The root expresses the idea of growth, enlargement, of what manifests in its power and extent.
H1436I.emploi: Gedaliah is mentioned twice, both in 1 Chronicles 25, at the heart of the cultic organization established by David. He represents a generation of Levitical musicians responsible for singing and instrumental music in the temple of Jerusalem. Unlike another Gedaliah who would become governor of Judah after the Babylonian exile (mentioned in Jeremiah and 2 Kings, but absent from these verses), this one belongs to the time of united Israel and does not exceed the scope of temple ministry.

sens: Political leader of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah, during the time of the prophet Jeremiah
H1436J.detail: Gedaliah is one of the influential leaders of Jerusalem during Jeremiah's ministry. He is the son of the priest Pashhur and is among the dignitaries who oppose the prophet and want to silence him, notably by throwing him into a cistern.
H1436J.origine: The name means "Jehovah is great" or "God is great" in Hebrew, composed of "gedol" (great) and "Yah" (God). It is a typical theophoric name of the ancient Near East, proclaiming divine greatness.
H1436J.emploi: Gedaliah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 38:1, where he appears with other leaders of Jerusalem who listen to the words that Jeremiah addresses to the people. Although not detailed in this passage, he represents the opposition of religious and political authorities against the prophet's message at the time of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar.

sens: Son of the seer Heman, belonging to the tribe of Levi during the divided monarchy of Israel
H1437.detail: Guiddalthi is a Levite, son of the prophet Heman who served the king. He is one of the thirteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chronicles 25:4, all destined to serve in the temple worship as musicians and singers. His name means "I make great" or "I enlarge." In 1 Chronicles 25:29, he is mentioned again as being in charge of the twenty-second division of service at the temple, along with his sons and brothers — which shows that he held an official and hereditary role in the organization of Levitical worship.
H1437.origine: The name Guiddalthi comes from the Hebrew giddal, which means "to make great" or "to enlarge." It is an action verb that expresses the idea of elevation or enlargement. The name thus carries a prophetic or programmatic meaning: one who "makes great," which could reflect the hopes of the parents or a particular calling.
H1437.emploi: Guiddalthi appears twice in 1 Chronicles 25, within the complete list of Heman's sons destined for the musical service of the temple. In 1 Chronicles 25:4, he is simply listed among his thirteen brothers. In 1 Chronicles 25:29, he reappears with a more defined role: he is assigned to the twenty-second watch for the worship services, accompanied by his sons and brothers, twelve in total. These two mentions confirm that he was an active participant in the official worship in the temple of Jerusalem.

sens: To cut, chop, break something solid (wood, stone, metal)
To demolish, overturn a durable construction or object
To annihilate, break the power or strength of someone
To cut off, remove, deprive of something
H1438.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of cutting or chopping something resistant: one "cuts down" wood with an axe, one "breaks" iron. It is the physical act of dividing by force.
2. It then applies to the destruction of objects or constructions: overturning an altar, demolishing a statue. In Deuteronomy 7:5, the Israelites are to "cut down" the idols of the nations, meaning to destroy them completely.
3. The word also expresses the annihilation of power or authority: the strength of Moab is "cut down" (Jeremiah 48:25), the pride of the king of Babylon is "brought down" to the ground (Isaiah 14:12). It is to break someone in their power.
4. Finally, it can mean to cut off, remove, deprive: God threatens to "cut off" the arm of the house of Eli (1 Samuel 2:31), meaning to take away its strength and its descendants.
H1438.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that paints the image of a sharp and violent blow that divides. It is related to the idea of separation and rupture: when one "cuts down" something, one divides it in two, separating it from its initial state. The word is used in all contexts where something must be broken by force — whether it be wood, stone, a cult object, or even, figuratively, a power or authority.
H1438.emploi: This verb appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books and the prophets. It almost always describes the action of destroying or annihilating: the Israelites "cut down" the altars and idols of false gods (Deuteronomy 7:5; 2 Chronicles 34:4), the prophets announce that God will "break" the doors and bars (Psalms 107:16), that the power of the nations will be "cut down" (Isaiah 10:33; Jeremiah 48:25). Figuratively, it is to break the strength or pride of someone, to "cut off" meaning to deprive them of their power. The context is always one of a violent, definitive rupture, often related to divine judgment.
H1438.portee: This verb reminds the reader that God has the power to break anything that opposes Him, whether it be false gods, unjust systems, or the pride of the powerful. It invites believers to radically destroy within themselves what diverts them from God, rather than tolerating it. It is also a promise of judgment: no human power can resist the will of God when it is manifested.

sens: Judge of Israel who led the people against the Midianites
Warrior chosen by God to deliver Israel
Man of little confidence who became a military leader
H1439.detail:
1. Gideon is the fifth judge of Israel, called by God to fight against the Midianites who oppressed the people. Son of Joash from the family of Abiezer, he is initially an ordinary young man, threshing wheat at the winepress (Judges 6:11), before the angel of the Lord comes to call him to this mission.

2. He becomes a renowned warrior who leads Israel to victory. With only three hundred men chosen by God through a special selection, he achieves a great victory: his soldiers blow the trumpet and shout "For the Lord and for Gideon!" (Judges 7:18), which puts the Midianite army to flight.

3. Gideon shows fragile confidence: he asks God for signs, like a wet fleece then a dry one, to confirm the divine calling (Judges 6:36-40). Despite his initial doubts, he obeys and becomes the deliverer of Israel, restoring peace to the land for forty years.
H1439.origine: The name Gideon means "hewer" or "one who cuts," evoking a man who slices, who acts with strength. He bears a second name, Jerubbaal ("let Baal contend"), given after he overturned Baal's altar, showing that his identity is inseparable from his calling as a champion against idolatry.
H1439.emploi: Gideon appears 37 times in the book of Judges, primarily in chapters 6 to 8. His story recounts how God transforms him: from a simple wheat thresher, afraid of the Midianites, he becomes a military leader whom the people beg to rule over them (Judges 8:22). The Bible emphasizes his humility — he refuses the kingship, stating that "the Lord will be your king" (Judges 8:23) — and the grace of God that works through the weak. After his death, the people quickly forget his devotion and return to idolatry (Judges 8:33-35).
H1439.portee: Gideon teaches that God calls ordinary people, full of fears and doubts, to accomplish His works. His initial weakness is not an obstacle: God transforms it through faith and obedience. His refusal of kingship reminds the reader that only the Lord should reign, and his story shows how true victory comes not from the strength of numbers, but from trust in God.

sens: Place between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon, in the territory of Benjamin
H1440.detail: 1. Guideom is a location where the Israelites halted their pursuit of the Benjaminites during the civil war recounted in chapter 20 of Judges. It is there that they killed two thousand men who were fleeing toward the desert and the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:45).
H1440.origine: The Hebrew name Guideom literally means "a cup" or "a section," evoking a marked or delineated area. Its etymology suggests a narrow passage or a well-defined crossing point in the terrain of the Benjaminite territory.
H1440.emploi: Guideom appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 20:45, in the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. This passage mentions it as the last point of pursuit of the Benjaminites who were fleeing toward the rock of Rimmon after their military defeat. Its exact location remains uncertain, but ancient sources place it between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon, in the mountainous regions of Benjamin.

sens: Father of Abidan, prince of the tribe of Benjamin
H1441.detail: Guideoni is a man from the tribe of Benjamin living during the time of the Exodus and in the wilderness. He is known only as the father of Abidan, who was designated as prince (chief) of his tribe. Abidan represented the sons of Benjamin during the census at Sinai (Numbers 1:11), during the organization of the camp (Numbers 2:22), and during the presentation of the offerings of the princes at the sanctuary (Numbers 7:60-65). Guideoni is mentioned again in Numbers 10:24 when Abidan, his son, commands the rear guard of the people's march in the wilderness.
H1441.origine: The Hebrew name means "my cutter" or "one who cuts," from a root evoking the action of chiseling or dividing. This type of patronymic name was common in Israel to identify a man in relation to his son or his activity.
H1441.emploi: Guideoni appears only five times in the Bible, always as the father of Abidan. He is mentioned during the first census of Israel at the foot of Sinai (Numbers 1:11), then in the context of the positioning of the tribes around the sanctuary (Numbers 2:22) and especially during the solemn presentation of the offerings of each tribal prince over twelve days (Numbers 7:60, 7:65). He appears a final time during the organization of the march in the wilderness (Numbers 10:24). These mentions show that Guideoni, although obscure, was respected as the father of a recognized tribal leader.

sens: To insult someone with contemptuous and offensive words
To blaspheme against God, treating Him with contempt and impiety
To show disdain towards a person or a sacred authority
H1442.detail:
1. To outrage someone is to seriously insult them, covering them with hurtful and humiliating words. It is an aggressive act aimed at lowering a person's dignity. When the psalmist speaks of one "who insults and outrages me" (Psalms 44:17), he describes a brutal verbal attack directed against him.

2. To outrage God is to blaspheme Him: to treat Him with impious contempt, refusing His authority in words and actions. This goes far beyond a simple insult—it's an act of religious rebellion. When the king of Assyria outrages the Lord through his servants (2 Kings 19:6), he denies His power and sacred character.

3. Outrage is a deliberate affront, a hand raised against someone (Numbers 15:30). That is why one who outrages God "with a raised hand," that is, consciously and willingly, incurs the gravest divine judgment: he will be cut off from his people.
H1442.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of raising the hand or lifting something in defiance. The image is that of an insult thrown with arrogance, head held high, and that is why the text of Numbers 15:30 expressly mentions the raised hand. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word often translates this notion of sacrilegious insult.
H1442.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the Old Testament, mostly in contexts of political or religious conflict. Three occurrences concern the servants of the king of Assyria who outrage God by denying His power (2 Kings 19:6 and 2 Kings 19:22; Isaiah 37:6 and Isaiah 37:23). A fundamental usage is found in Numbers 15:30: one who outrages the Lord "with a raised hand" commits a grave sin that leads to his separation from the people. The psalmist also suffers the outrage of his enemies (Psalms 44:17). In Ezekiel 20:27, God reproaches Israel for having outraged His name through idolatry. Outrage always denotes an act of conscious and voluntary rebellion.
H1442.portee: This word reminds the believer that words carry serious spiritual weight: insulting the Lord is not a trivial act; it is a rebellion that engages our responsibility before God. It also warns us: the arrogance that manifests "with a raised hand" towards God or His servants is a path that leads to judgment. Conversely, this word helps us to entrust to God the outrages we endure, knowing that He sees and judges.

sens: to build a wall, to surround with a wall
to close access, to block passage
to repair, to restore
a person who builds or repairs a wall
H1443.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to build a wall of stone or bricks, surrounding a space to protect or delimit it. In Lamentations 3:7, the poet says, "He has surrounded me with a wall," which shows the concrete enclosure formed by this construction.
2. The word is also used figuratively to express the idea of closure, obstruction of passage: Job says, "He has closed off all my paths, and I cannot pass" (Job 19:8), describing how God blocks access as one would with a wall. Similarly, "He has closed my way with hewn stones" (Lamentations 3:9) illustrates spiritual confinement.
3. To restore or rebuild is a closely related meaning: to repair destroyed walls, to raise up what has fallen. Isaiah 58:12 calls Jerusalem to become "repairer of the breaches," one who stands up the ruins.
4. By metonymy, the word designates the mason or worker who builds walls (2 Kings 12:12, 22:6), one whose trade is to work with stone.
H1443.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּדַר (gadar) comes from a root evoking the idea of enclosure and boundary. It is from the same family as the noun גָּדֵר (gader, "wall, enclosure"). The basic image is that of a construction that separates, that divides space into inside and outside. This verb is used for both the concrete action and its metaphorical effect of confinement or restriction.
H1443.emploi: The verb appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in contexts of construction and restoration, or in the figurative sense of closure. In the kings (2 Kings 12:12, 22:6), it is used regarding the repair work of the Temple: masons and stone workers restore the house of the Lord. In the poets (Job, Lamentations, Isaiah), it takes on a spiritual hue: God "closes" the paths of His adversaries or of the suffering to block their hope. In Isaiah 58:12, it is a promise: the faithful will rebuild what has fallen. Ezekiel and Hosea use it regarding the breach of the wall of the Temple or that of Israel, a symbol of compromised divine protection.
H1443.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God has the power to close and open paths. It also teaches that the restoration of walls, in a spiritual sense, is the work of those who stand in the breach (Ezekiel 22:30) to intercede. Finally, it shows that the work of the faithful worker, even humble, participates in the service of the Temple and the Lord.

sens: Construction of stone or fill materials delimiting a space or protecting a property
Wall of an enclosure or building
Barrier, obstacle, limit
H1444.detail:
1. The wall is a tall construction that separates spaces and properties: it is a work of stone or piled materials. In Proverbs 24:31, the stone wall of a neglected field collapses, revealing the abandonment and negligence of the owner.
2. It is also the wall that delineates spaces within a building or enclosure. In Ezekiel 42:10, the wall of the temple courtyard is mentioned, that is, the partition or wall that forms the enclosure of this sacred place.
3. The wall can represent a separation, a limit, or an obstacle—something that stops, protects, or divides.
H1444.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to enclose" or "to delimit." The wall is by nature what creates a barrier, what encloses a space. It is a simple and very ancient word in Hebrew, used for both city walls and private property fences.
H1444.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to these provided usages. In Proverbs 24:31, it refers to the stone wall of the slothful that collapses, a symbol of ruin and decay. In Ezekiel 42:10, it refers to one of the walls of the temple of Jerusalem, in the precise description of the sacred building. The context changes—symbol of abandonment on one side, architectural element on the other—but the word retains its concrete meaning: a solid structure raised to delimit or protect.
H1444.portee: The collapsed stone wall in Proverbs invites the believer to meditate on the ruin that awaits laziness and lack of diligence: a wall does not fall without cause. It is a call to be vigilant in maintaining what has been entrusted to us, both materially and spiritually.

sens: City of Canaan conquered by Joshua
H1445.detail: Geder is a small Canaanite city whose king was defeated by Joshua during the conquest of the Promised Land. It appears in the list of thirty-one defeated kings (Joshua 12:13), between Debir and Hormah. Its name means "wall" in Hebrew, evoking the fortifications that protected it.
H1445.origine: The name Geder comes from the Hebrew geder, which literally means "wall" or "fence." It shares the same root found in the word "Gedor" (Gedor, H1446G), which sometimes refers to the same place or a neighboring locality. The name reflects the fortified nature of Canaanite cities of that time.
H1445.emploi: Geder appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 12:13, where it is mentioned as one of the thirty-one Canaanite cities whose kings were defeated by Joshua. The list in Joshua 12 summarizes all the victories won east and west of the Jordan, from King Sihon of Heshbon to the kings of the southern land. Geder, though little known, symbolizes the completeness of victory: no significant city escaped conquest.
H1445.portee: The mention of Geder reminds us that God's promise to Israel—the possession of the land—was realized in a concrete and total way. Every victory, even that of a small city, testifies to God's faithfulness and His accompaniment of the chosen people.

sens: fortified city of Judah, north of Hebron
place of origin of warriors
patronymic: father or ancestor
H1446G.detail: 1. Gedor is a mountain city located in the territory of Judah, a few kilometers north of Hebron. It appears in the list of cities conquered by the Israelites in the Promised Land (Joshua 15:58), indicating its importance as a territorial possession of Israel. 2. The city is associated with the origin of warriors and notable figures: the text of 1 Chronicles 12:7 mentions men from Gedor who joined David's forces, showing that it was a militarily active population center. 3. In the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, the name Gedor also appears as a patronymic—a person whose descendants are identified in relation to this ancestor (1 Chronicles 4:4 and 4:18), suggesting that the place was linked to an important lineage of Judah.
H1446G.origine: The Hebrew name גְּדוֹר (Gedor) literally means "wall" or "rampart," likely reflecting the defensive characteristic or fortified aspect of the site. This meaning is consistent with a mountain city intended to control and protect the territory. The word also appears in the form Geder (H1445) in the textual tradition.
H1446G.emploi: Gedor appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. First as a city in the territory of Judah annexed during the conquest (Joshua 15:58). It is then mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a name of a person or a patronymic associated with the descendants of Hur and the lineage of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:4 and 4:18). Finally, the text of 1 Chronicles 12:7 indicates that warriors from Gedor joined David, confirming that it was a strategically located population center in the mountains of Judah.

sens: city located east of the valley
place of pastures
H1446H.detail: Gedor is a city mentioned only once in Chronicles. In the time of the generations of Judah, some men went to Gedor to seek pastures for their flocks, indicating that it was a fertile region suitable for grazing (1 Chronicles 4:39).
H1446H.origine: The name literally means "wall" in Hebrew, probably because the city was fortified or built on a defensive site. This type of geographical name is common in ancient Israel, where walls served to protect human settlements.
H1446H.emploi: Gedor appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:39. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark to which cattle herders went to find pastures. The context suggests that it was a fertile region of the valley, likely to the east, accessible to the flocks of that time.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the united monarchy
H1446I.detail: 1. Gedor is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was united. He appears in the genealogical lists of the First Book of Chronicles, where he is mentioned twice consecutively: first in 1 Chronicles 8:31 as the son of Abiel, and then in 1 Chronicles 9:37 in a listing of the descendants of Gibeon (1 Chronicles 9:37).
H1446I.origine: The name Gedor means "wall" or "rampart" in Hebrew. It is an ancient name from Galilee, borne by several distinct people or places in the Old Testament. The provided text mentions at least one other Gedor: a city in the mountainous region of Judah, north of Hebron. The uses in Chronicles specifically refer to a man from the people of Benjamin during the united monarchy.
H1446I.emploi: Gedor is mentioned twice in the genealogical records of the First Book of Chronicles, always in the company of his brothers: Ahijah and Zechariah. These two occurrences (1 Chronicles 8:31 and 9:37) suggest that they are parallel genealogies, perhaps two versions of the same family list. He is presented as the son of Abiel and brother of Kish, Ner, and several others, integrating him into a Benjaminite genealogical line. His name does not appear elsewhere in the provided biblical texts.

sens: Structure of stone or wood that encloses and protects a space
Boundary or protection around a vineyard or field
Refuge, place of shelter or safety
Breach or weakness in a defense
H1447.detail: 1. In its primary sense, a fence is a construction that surrounds a space: stone or wood assembled to form a barrier. In Numbers 22:24, the angel stands "in a path between the vineyards; there was a wall on either side," where the two fences delimit and enclose the passage. 2. Specifically, it protects vineyards and fields from animals and thieves. Isaiah 5:5 speaks of the Lord's vineyard: "I will tear down its fence, so that it will be trampled down," showing that the fence was the guardian of this fragile wealth. 3. Figuratively, it signifies a refuge or spiritual protection. Ezra 9:9 states that God gave the exiles "a retreat in Judah and Jerusalem"—a fence that isolates them and keeps them safe after captivity. 4. By extension, a broken or overturned fence represents abandonment, vulnerability. Psalms 80:13 cries out: "Why have you broken down its fences?" expressing dismay at the ruin of Israel.
H1447.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to surround" or "to encircle." It designates any barrier built to separate, protect, or delimit a space—stone, wood, or intertwined hedge. The same root has produced a neighboring word (geder, H1444) which is also a fence or wall. It is a concrete and everyday term in the agricultural and urban life of the ancient Near East.
H1447.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophets and poems. In Numbers 22:24, it is a physical fence that delineates a mountain path. In Isaiah 5:5 and Hosea 2:8, it surrounds the vineyard—the image of Israel well guarded by God. Ezekiel uses the word to speak of one who "stands in the breach" (Ezekiel 22:30), where the broken fence becomes the image of a nation without spiritual defense. In Ezra 9:9, the fence takes on a sense of refuge or safe territory given by Providence. Its meaning varies from the concrete (a stone construction) to the spiritual (the protection or lack of protection of Israel).
H1447.portee: This image of the fence invites the believer to meditate on divine protection: God surrounds His people to preserve them, but this protection requires faithfulness and obedience. When the fence is broken, it is a sign of abandonment or judgment. It also reminds us that the Christian life needs boundaries—separations from evil—to grow safely.

sens: Fence or enclosure made of stone or wood intended to contain livestock
Hedge or wall serving as a boundary or protection
Fortress or stronghold
H1448.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a defined and closed space to contain flocks. Thus, in Numbers 32:16, the tribes ask Moses for permission to "build enclosures for our livestock" — solid enclosures that shelter sheep and goats. In 1 Samuel 24:4, David hides in a cave near the "sheep enclosures," that is, sheepfolds or enclosures that mark the terrain.
2. By extension, the word refers to any wall or hedge that creates a barrier, a protective limit. Psalm 89:41 speaks of the "walls" destroyed of a city, the defensive structures that have been torn down. It is the same idea of enclosure, but applied to civil or military architecture rather than to livestock.
3. In the context of war or politics, it can refer to a stronghold or fortress — the idea of "enclosure" remains that of an enclosure, but has become a symbol of defense and power. Jeremiah 49:3 mentions the "walls" of Rabbah: it is the enclosure that has become an urban fortification.
H1448.origine: The Hebrew word גְּדֵרָה (gédérah) comes from the root גדר (gadar), which means "to enclose, to fence, to make a hedge." It expresses the action of erecting a barrier, of delimiting a space. The word concretely evokes the image of a fence built with stones or branches, the very action of delimiting and protecting. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to walls and fences.
H1448.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. In Numbers 32:16, 32:24, and 32:36, it refers to enclosures for livestock — the Reubenites and Gadites ask to build "enclosures" for their flocks. In 1 Samuel 24:4, the context of the sheep confirms this meaning. However, in Psalm 89:41 and Jeremiah 49:3, the word applies to the "walls" of conquered or threatened cities, showing that the meaning broadens to cover any defensive enclosure. The common notion is that of a delimitation, a closed enclosure, whether it protects flocks or fortifies a city.
H1448.portee: This word reminds us that the Old Testament honors the humble work of shepherds and herders, who build enclosures to protect their livestock — a daily and vital task. It also shows that a fence, an enclosure, a wall represents protection and stability: what is enclosed is safe. For the believer, this evokes the idea that God Himself can be a rampart, a protection that limits us to keep us safe.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Judah in the Lowlands
H1449.detail: 1. Gederah was a fortified city (its name literally means "wall" or "enclosure") located in the low region of Judah, towards the foothills that descend to the coastal plain. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the land (Joshua 15:36), alongside other localities in the same area.
H1449.origine: The Hebrew word גְּדֵרָה (gederah) comes from the root גָּדַר (gadar), which means "to enclose" or "to fence," hence "wall" or "enclosure." This is why this name describes a city protected by walls, a common characteristic of settlements of that time. The term is related to other Hebrew words for "fence" (gadér) and "shepherd" (gadî).
H1449.emploi: Gederah is mentioned twice in the biblical texts that have come down to us: first in Joshua 15:36, where it appears in the enumeration of cities in the territory of Judah assigned during the conquest of the promised land, and then in 1 Chronicles 4:23, where it is cited in another historical list. It was a city in the low region of Judah, that is, the less mountainous area closer to the coastal plain, unlike the cities in the mountain of Judah.

sens: City of the lowlands of Judah
H1450.detail: 1. Gederoth is a fortified city located in the lowlands (the Shephelah) of southern Judah, listed among the cities of the territory of Judah. Its name itself means "walls" or "enclosure" in Hebrew, suggesting a place protected by fortifications. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Judah after the conquest (Joshua 15:41), grouped with Beth-Dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah. In the time of King Ahaz, Gederoth experienced the humiliation of being conquered by the Philistines during their invasion of the lowlands and the Negev of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:18), testifying to the vulnerability of border cities to neighboring powers.
H1450.origine: The name Gederoth comes from the Hebrew root "gader" (גדר) which means "wall" or "fence." The word literally designates a closed or protected place by walls, which perfectly suits a fortress or a fortified city in the lowlands. This etymology reflects the strategic importance of fortifications in the military architecture of Judah.
H1450.emploi: Gederoth appears only twice in the Bible, always in the form "Gederoth." First mentioned in Joshua 15:41 as one of the sixteen cities allocated to the tribe of Judah in the Shephelah (the low hills), it is then cited in 2 Chronicles 28:18, where it is listed among the lowland and southern cities captured by the Philistines under Ahaz. These two occurrences show that Gederoth was a stable but vulnerable possession of Judah, located in a border area.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Geder
H1451.detail: This word designates an inhabitant of Geder, a city of ancient Israel. In the only passage where it appears, Baal-Hanan, identified as Geder, is responsible for the olive trees and sycamores in the plain under the reign of King David (1 Chronicles 27:28). It is a geographical title that identifies the origin or function of this person in the royal administration.
H1451.origine: The word comes from Geder (גְּדֵרָה), whose name means "wall" or "enclosure" in Hebrew. This likely evokes a city protected by walls, characteristic of fortified cities in Canaan. The suffix -ri adds the idea of belonging, transforming the name of the city into a demonym ("inhabitant of"), similar to how one says "French" for an inhabitant of France.
H1451.emploi: This demonym appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:28. Baal-Hanan, identified as Geder, holds a position of authority in the agricultural administration of King David, responsible for overseeing the olive trees and sycamores of the plain. His mere mention shows the importance of this role in the economy of the kingdom, where oil harvests were a major wealth.
H1451.portee: This passage offers a glimpse into the careful and efficient organization of David's kingdom: even the officials responsible for agricultural resources are named and documented. It reminds the reader that God also values humble work and faithful administration of material goods, not just spectacular acts.

sens: City in the territory of Judah in the Old Testament
H1452.detail: Gederah is a city of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 12:4 as the place of origin of Jozabad, one of the warriors who came to join David at Ziklag. The name literally means "wall" or "enclosure," perhaps evoking fortifications or a city surrounded by walls, like many cities in southern Judea.
H1452.origine: The name Gederah comes from the Hebrew root "gâder" (גָּדַר), which means "to make a fence, to build a wall." The suffix "-ah" (הָ) forms the name of the place. It is a real location in ancient Judea, distinct from the larger Gedor mentioned elsewhere.
H1452.emploi: Gederah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:4. It is cited as the birthplace of Jozabad, a valiant warrior who was part of David's companions when he was gathering his forces. This context shows that Gederah was a locality in the territory of Judah significant enough to be the seat of families of warriors.

sens: City in the low region of Judah
H1453.detail: Guedérothaïm is a small town located in the low and fertile region of Judah, in the southwest of the territory. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:36).
H1453.origine: The name means 'two walls' or 'two enclosures' in Hebrew, probably referring to fortifications or a characteristic defensive structure of the place. It is a descriptive name that highlights the strategic or architectural importance of the site.
H1453.emploi: Guedérothaïm is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:36, in the enumeration of the cities of the lot of Judah. It is cited among other small localities in the low region (Schaaraim and Adithaim notably) in a group of fourteen cities with their respective villages. This mention is part of the account of the division of the land among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Particle pointing to what has just been said or what will be stated
Marks a transition or a solemn announcement
H1454.detail:
1. This Hebrew particle designates what is immediately present in the discourse — what has just been mentioned or what will be. It functions as a gesture that directs attention: 'here is' or 'what follows'. In Ezekiel 47:13, the prophet announces 'Here are the borders of the land': the particle geh prepares the precise enumeration of the boundaries that will follow, as if God were pointing to the map of the promised territory.
2. It often serves to open a prophetic or official word, marking a moment of particular importance. It is equivalent to 'listen' or a knock to attract attention before a significant declaration.
H1454.origine: This particle comes from ancient Hebrew and has a very close Aramaic equivalent: da (דָּא 'this'). It is related to the Hebrew root that expresses designation or presentation. Its basic image is that of a finger pointing: it materializes in language the gesture of indicating something clearly and immediately.
H1454.emploi: This particle appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Ezekiel 47:13, where it serves to announce a divine word. God addresses Ezekiel to convey the precise outlines of the territory that the twelve tribes will share. The word geh marks here the introduction of a concrete spatial revelation: the borders of the land that had been promised to Abraham and his descendants. It is a clearly declarative, solemn usage.
H1454.portee: This small particle reminds us that God speaks with clarity and precision. When He says 'here is', it is so that no one is mistaken: He unfolds His will in a visible and deliberate manner. For the reader, this invites attention and respect: when God shows, it is because He is showing something important.

sens: That which heals a disease or a wound
That which resolves a problem or a moral evil
H1455.detail:
1. The word primarily designates that which heals and cures a wound or a disease of the body. In Hosea 5:13, the prophet says that the king of Assyria cannot 'bring remedy to your wounds': the wounds of the unfaithful people cannot be healed by political alliances, as they are primarily spiritual.
2. Figuratively, it is the solution to a deeper evil: a rupture with God. The text shows that only a moral and spiritual healing can truly save Judah and Ephraim.
H1455.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּהָה (gahah) literally means 'to depart' or 'to go away'. In this context, the idea is that the disease goes away, that it disappears. The word thus approaches the image of healing as a departure from evil: when one is healed, the evil 'leaves'. It is a figurative thought, characteristic of ancient languages.
H1455.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 5:13. The prophet Hosea uses it to reproach the northern (Ephraim) and southern (Judah) kingdoms for seeking political help in Assyria, while they need spiritual healing. The word is used in the sense of 'solution' or 'remedy' to moral and religious wounds. This unique occurrence highlights the importance of the passage: Hosea insists that no diplomacy is a remedy for sin.
H1455.portee: This word reminds believers that true wounds are spiritual and that only God can heal them. Seeking help from other powers or other gods is vain; true healing comes from returning to God. It is a call not to confuse the appearances of salvation with salvation itself.

sens: That which heals a disease or alleviates suffering
That which restores, puts back in good condition
That which restores health to the heart and mind
H1456.detail:
1. The remedy is primarily that which heals the sick or wounded body, that which brings back physical health. In Proverbs 17:22, it is the image of medicine: 'A cheerful heart is a good remedy'.
2. More broadly, it is that which restores, which puts in order what was deficient or damaged. The word applies to healing in a broad sense, whether physical or inner.
3. In this passage, the remedy is particularly spiritual and emotional: the joy of the heart heals like medicine, while 'a crushed spirit dries up the bones', meaning it weakens life itself. The remedy opposes what destroys.
H1456.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of healing, restoring. It literally designates that which brings back to health, the cure or the healing itself. It is a rare word in the Hebrew Bible.
H1456.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 17:22. It is used in a figurative and spiritual sense: the sincere joy of the heart acts as a powerful remedy for the whole being, while discouragement destroys it. It is a medical image applied to inner life.
H1456.portee: This verse teaches the reader that their emotional and spiritual state has real consequences on their health and well-being. Joy is not a luxury, but an essential remedy; it comes from the heart and spreads throughout our being. Conversely, bitterness and discouragement eat away at us from the inside. Cultivating joy in the Lord is therefore an act of wisdom and self-care.

sens: To incline one's body downward or forward
To lie down on someone or stretch out over them
To adopt a posture of humility or supplication before God
H1457.detail:
1. The verb first describes the physical gesture of leaning one's body: Elijah 'bends down to the ground' and puts his face between his knees in prayer at the top of Carmel (1 Kings 18:42), showing a posture of concentration and fervor.
2. It also means to stretch out or lie down on someone: Elisha 'stretches out' over the dead child to warm him with the contact of his body (2 Kings 4:34-35), transmitting vital warmth through close physical proximity.
3. In these religious contexts, leaning expresses a spiritual attitude: that of the supplicant who humbles themselves before God or that of the prophet who seeks to transmit divine life.
H1457.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּהַר (gahar) belongs to a family of words evoking the inclination and bending of the body. Its basic image is that of movement downward: one leans, bends, or lowers oneself. This verb appears only a few times in the Bible, always in contexts rich with spiritual or miraculous meaning.
H1457.emploi: The verb gahar appears three times in the Old Testament, only in the books of Kings. It designates each time a concrete gesture but rich in religious significance: Elijah leans in fervent prayer to ask for rain (1 Kings 18:42), and Elisha stretches out twice over the Shunammite's child to resurrect him (2 Kings 4:34-35). The word retains its literal physical meaning – an inclination or extension of the body – but in each usage, this bodily gesture becomes the means by which the prophet seeks to touch the invisible: the action of God.
H1457.portee: This verb reminds us that fervent prayer engages the whole body, not just the spirit. The example of Elijah showing how to lean, how to physically humble oneself, invites the believer to an embodied prayer. The gestures of Elisha also reveal that God often acts through contact, through proximity, through our engaged presence with others: spiritual life is never abstract.

sens: the rear part of the human body
to reject or abandon something by putting it behind oneself
H1458.detail:
1. The back is the rear part of the body, between the shoulders and the lower back. This is the physical and concrete meaning of the word.
2. To put something "behind one's back" means to set it aside, to willfully forget it, to reject it as unimportant. The image is of someone turning their back on what they abandon. In 1 Kings 14:9, the king "rejects behind his back" the God of Israel by turning to other gods. In Nehemiah 9:26 and Ezekiel 23:35, the people or the queen "throw the law behind their back" to signify that they willfully ignore it and refuse to obey it.
H1458.origine: The Hebrew word "gav" literally refers to the back, the rear part of the body. This part of the body, which is not seen when one turns elsewhere, naturally becomes a symbol of what is forgotten or rejected. The expression "behind the back" exists in both Hebrew and French to express abandonment or contempt.
H1458.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the figurative sense of abandonment or rejection. The three uses are found in contexts of disobedience towards God or His law: a king who rejects the God of Israel (1 Kings 14:9), the people who reject the divine law (Nehemiah 9:26), a queen who forgets God (Ezekiel 23:35). The expression "behind the back" is consistent in these three verses, always describing an act of unfaithfulness or rebellion.
H1458.portee: Putting God "behind one's back" is the biblical image of unfaithfulness: it is willfully turning one's back on the one known and rejecting His will. This image helps the believer understand that idolatry or disobedience are not mere mistakes, but deliberate choices to forget and despise God.

sens: The central place of a space, surrounded on all sides
The heart or inner part of something
What separates or divides into two parts
The center of an action or event
H1459.detail:
1. The middle is the central space, the place where one is surrounded on all sides. When the three young Hebrews are threatened with being thrown "into the middle of a fiery furnace" (Daniel 3:6), they would be plunged into the fire, right at the heart of the flames. The word precisely evokes this central point of the blazing furnace.
2. The middle can also refer to the heart or inner part of something, what constitutes it from the inside. The tree in Nebuchadnezzar's dream stands "in the middle of the earth" (Daniel 4:10), occupying the central place in the visible landscape. The word speaks of an imposing presence at the center.
3. It can mean what separates or divides, what stands between two things or two parts. In the Aramaic text of the Scriptures, the word also carries the meaning of "rebellion" or "tumult," expressing agitation that divides and troubles (Ezra 4:15).
4. Finally, the middle can refer to the context or very place of an event: it is "in the middle of the fire" that the three men walk unharmed (Daniel 3:25), not at the periphery, but at the heart of divine action.
H1459.origine: The Aramaic word "gav" comes from a root that means the central space, the hollow or inside of something. Its Hebrew equivalent "gev" (גֵּו) carries the same meaning of "middle" or "inside." This root evokes the idea of what is at the heart, at the center, surrounded by other elements. The transition from Hebrew to the Aramaic dialect in the later chapters of Daniel and Ezra did not change the fundamental meaning of the word.
H1459.emploi: The Aramaic word "gav" appears 13 times in the Bible, only in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which are partially written in Aramaic. Its primary usage is spatial: "in the middle of the fire" (Daniel 3:25), "in the middle of the furnace" (Daniel 3:6, 3:15, 3:23). In Ezra, the word takes on a different nuance: in Ezra 4:15, "gav" is translated as "rebellion," expressing agitation or trouble that divides. The context shows that the word retains its meaning of center or heart: the heart of the problem, what stirs at the center of the city. This nuance reflects the Aramaic usage where the word can mean both the physical space and the essence of a situation.
H1459.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God's presence is manifested in the "middle" of the most extreme trials. The three young Hebrews are not simply spared: it is in the heart of the fire, "in the middle" of the flames, that the Son of God walks with them (Daniel 3:25). This teaches that divine protection does not isolate from danger, but accompanies us within the danger itself. The word invites us to seek the Lord not by fleeing trials, but by finding Him at the very center of our struggles.

sens: the rear part of the human body
blow or corporal punishment
what is behind, rejected
H1460A.detail:
1. The back is the rear part of the human body, from the neck to the lower back. It is the area struck by the whip or rod: "The rod is for the back of the fool" (Proverbs 10:13). The exposed back symbolizes vulnerability and submission to correction.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the blows themselves, the corporal punishment inflicted on the back. The verbs "strike the back," "deliver the back," express the idea of receiving correction or physical violence: "I gave my back to those who struck me" (Isaiah 50:6), where the prophet willingly accepts humiliation.
3. In a figurative sense, the back represents what is abandoned, what is thrown behind oneself, what is rejected or forgotten. In Isaiah 38:17, God "throws" the sins of the sick man behind Him, meaning He erases and rejects them far away.
H1460A.origine: The Hebrew word "gev" comes from a root that designates the curved or bent body. The back is naturally the part of the body that bends when one leans or submits. The word is first used in a physical and concrete sense, then expands to the idea of rejection or abandonment, as throwing something behind one's back means rejecting it from sight and mind.
H1460A.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, first in Proverbs (three occurrences) where it speaks of the rod applied to the backs of fools, a teaching on correction. In Isaiah, it takes on a deeper spiritual significance: the suffering servant gives his back to the blows (Isaiah 50:6), an image of humiliation and accepted suffering; the back also becomes the symbol of sin thrown behind God (Isaiah 38:17) or of bodies humiliated under the foot of the oppressor (Isaiah 51:23). The meaning oscillates between the concrete physical and the figurative spiritual.
H1460A.portee: For the believer, the back of the suffering servant in Isaiah 50:6 foreshadows Christ who accepts suffering. The image of throwing sins behind oneself (Isaiah 38:17) teaches that God's forgiveness is radical: He does not keep the memory of our faults. Finally, Proverbs reminds us that correction, although painful, is an act of love aimed at restoring the one who has gone astray.

sens: The space located between two or more things, at the center
H1460B.detail: 1. This word designates the center or the space that is found in the middle of a larger reality. In Job 30:5, it refers to the middle of the inhabited world, the society of men: the poor and the unfortunate are "driven away," rejected far from the center of common life. It is the image of social exclusion and marginalization.
H1460B.origine: The Hebrew word "gev" comes from a common Semitic root that expresses the idea of the center or the inside. The very close Aramaic word "gav" (H1459) carries the same meaning. It is a simple, concrete word that primarily evokes the empty space at the heart of something.
H1460B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible at this location. It properly designates the central space or the heart of a larger reality. In Job 30:5, it refers to the middle of civil life, of the human community, to say that some are excluded from it. It is a natural and direct term, without particular connotation.
H1460B.portee: This passage invites us to see those whom society marginalizes. Job reminds us that men are rejected "from the middle" — they are no longer part of the world of the living who are integrated. It is a call not to forget the excluded and the despised.

sens: winged insect that moves in jumps and flies in large masses
here: immense multitude of locusts gathered
H1462A.detail:
1. The word refers to the locust, an insect characterized by its powerful hind legs that allow it to jump very high and far, and which often travels in gigantic swarms capable of devastating lands (Nahum 3:17).
2. In the passage from Nahum, the prophet speaks of the princes as if they were an innumerable multitude of locusts: the word evokes both their overwhelming number and their instability, as locusts take flight and disappear in an instant.
H1462A.origine: The Hebrew word gôv is a variant of gibay (or gobay), which belongs to the family of names designating pest insects. In Hebrew, several distinct terms refer to different types of locusts or grasshoppers, reflecting the importance of these creatures in Middle Eastern agriculture. The word captures the image of what flies away, scatters, and eludes sight.
H1462A.emploi: The word appears only once in the received biblical text, in Nahum 3:17, where the prophet denounces the princes of Nineveh. He compares them to locusts that settle on the hedges in the cold, then take flight when the sun appears: a striking image of sudden disappearance and helplessness. The metaphor emphasizes that despite their apparent number, these leaders have no solidity and will vanish like insects at the first gust of divine judgment.
H1462A.portee: This comparison invites the reader not to fear enemy powers, no matter how numerous they may be: they are ephemeral and fragile in the face of God's justice. For the persecuted believer, it is a message of hope: the oppressors, even in legions, are but locusts in the eyes of the Lord.

sens: winged insect with an elongated body, capable of jumping and flying
sign of divine judgment on Israel
symbol of the fragility and disappearance of the powerful
H1462B.detail:
1. The locust is a well-known insect in the ancient Near East: it has an elongated body, wings that allow it to fly, and powerful legs that enable it to jump. It is an insect that moves in swarms and can devastate crops (Amos 7:1 shows locusts multiplying supernaturally at the time of the first shoots).
2. In Amos's vision, the Lord sends the locusts as an act of judgment on Israel, to punish it. It is one of the plagues that God uses to warn His people.
3. In Nahum 3:17, locusts symbolize the fragility of the powerful: the princes and leaders of Assyria are compared to locusts that take flight as soon as the sun rises, disappearing without a trace. It is the image of the ephemeral, of one who thinks he is strong but vanishes before God's judgment.
H1462B.origine: The Hebrew word גֹּבַי comes from a root that specifically designates the insect. It is an ancient and simple term to name this insect well-known in the biblical world. Locusts were known for their massive and destructive invasions in Egypt and the Levant, which is why the Bible uses them as a symbol of judgment and devastation.
H1462B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, at two decisive moments when locusts become symbols of God's judgment. In Amos's vision (7:1), they are sent by the Lord Himself as a means to strike Israel, in a warning vision addressed to the prophet. In Nahum (3:17), they serve as a comparison to show how Assyria, despite its apparent power, will also disappear as quickly as a swarm of locusts that take flight. Both uses play on the contrast between the fearsome appearance of the swarm and its volatility.
H1462B.portee: The locusts remind us that God's judgment is concrete and visible, not an abstract idea. They also symbolize the fragility of any human power that opposes God: even empires that seem invincible last only an instant under the Lord's gaze. It is a call not to place our trust in what disappears.

sens: Man of the tribe of Reuben, son of Schemaiah
H1463G.detail: Gog is a descendant of Reuben mentioned only once in the genealogy of the sons of Reuben. He is the son of Schemaiah and the father of Shimei, placing his life in the time of Egypt and the wilderness (1 Chronicles 5:4). His name literally means "mountain."
H1463G.origine: The name Gog comes from a Hebrew root meaning "mountain." This same name appears in the prophecies of Ezekiel to designate a future warrior prince from the lands of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, although it is in a prophetic context distinct from this historical Reubenite.
H1463G.emploi: Gog appears only once in the Bible in a historical sense: in 1 Chronicles 5:4, where he is listed as a link in a genealogy of the tribe of Reuben. This passage enumerates the family heads and their descendants, placing Gog in the continuity of the patriarchal lines of the Old Testament. No account details his life or deeds.

sens: Military and political leader of a power hostile to Israel
Earthly power that opposes the people of God
H1463H.detail: Gog is a character or leader presented in the book of Ezekiel as prince of Rosch, Meshech, and Tubal, regions located north of Israel. He represents a major military power advancing against the land of Israel to attack it, according to a prophetic vision of divine judgment (Ezekiel 38:2-3). In this prophecy, God directly opposes Gog and promises to fight against him to manifest Himself as holy before the nations (Ezekiel 38:16). Gog thus symbolizes the earthly enemy that challenges the chosen people, but whose destiny is ultimately controlled by God.
H1463H.origine: The name "Gog" historically or prophetically designates a leader or territory in the ancient Near Eastern world. Although the exact etymology remains debated, the definition underscores a connection with northern regions: Rosch, Meshech, and Tubal. The name appears concentrated in the book of Ezekiel, where it plays a central role in the eschatological prophecies concerning the last days of the people of Israel.
H1463H.emploi: Gog primarily appears in chapters 38 and 39 of Ezekiel, where the prophet is commanded to prophesy against him six times. Gog is always presented as a powerful prince who gathers a coalition of peoples to march against Israel. God directly addresses Gog (Ezekiel 38:3, 38:14), confronts him with His fury (Ezekiel 38:18), and announces his imminent defeat (Ezekiel 39:1). This figure embodies the ultimate threat against the people of God, but also the opportunity for the Lord to demonstrate His holiness and power over all nations.
H1463H.portee: Gog represents for the biblical reader the reality of spiritual conflict: an arrogant earthly power that believes it can crush the people of God, but which collides with divine sovereignty. This prophecy reminds us that God controls history and even the plans of Israel's enemies serve ultimate intentions: the revelation of His holiness. It invites the believer to an unwavering trust in God, even in the face of the most imposing threats.

sens: Attack by surprise with an armed group
Rush at someone to fight them
Invade a territory
H1464.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to attack by surprise with an armed group: it is a rapid and violent incursion, like that of a band of warriors. In Genesis 49:19, the patriarch Jacob prophesies that the tribe of Gad will be "assailed" by armed bands, but that it will respond by "assailing" its enemies and pursuing them.
2. More broadly, the word describes the action of rushing at someone to fight, with the idea of an immediate and pressing threat. In Habakkuk 3:16, the prophet speaks of the "oppressor" who will march against the people: here, the word evokes less a raid than a threatening invasion, that of an invader advancing against the nation.
H1464.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pushing, rushing forward. The underlying image is that of a troop charging, rushing toward a target. The word belongs to the military vocabulary of the Old Testament, where surprise attacks and raids are common.
H1464.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 49:19, it describes the offensive-defensive cycle: Gad will be attacked, but will counterattack. In Habakkuk 3:16, in a prophetic context of anguish in the face of invasion, the word takes on a more serious and existential shade. In both cases, it involves battles on a tribal or national scale, not mere skirmishes.
H1464.portee: This word reminds the reader that threats against God's people are not passive: one can be "assailed," yes, but also retaliate and pursue the enemy. For Habakkuk, it invites reflection on the reality of spiritual and political combat while awaiting divine judgment.

sens: The interior of the body, the deep organs
What is hidden within, one's secret or hidden intention
H1465.detail:
1. The word designates the internal organs of the body, the seat of emotions and life. In Job 20:25, it is literally the belly of the wicked that is pierced by the arrow — the image evokes the mortal wound that strikes a man at his very core.
2. Figuratively, the bowels represent the secret heart of a person, where true feelings and real intentions are tied. It is from the innermost being that suffering and fear arise.
H1465.origine: The Hebrew word גֵּוָה comes from a root that means "back" or "behind," but the context of Job categorizes it among the words designating the interior of the body. In Hebrew, the interior of the body — the heart, the kidneys, the bowels — is always the seat of moral and spiritual life, not just physical. It is a deeply existential lexicon: what happens in the bowels reveals the soul.
H1465.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in this sense. The passage in Job 20:25 describes the punishment of the wicked: God's arrow pierces his bowels, taking away his strength and protection. It is an image of total judgment, reaching the man to his very essence. The context shows that the bowels are the last refuge, one that cannot be defended — and it is there that punishment falls.
H1465.portee: This word reminds us that God does not judge only our external acts, but reaches to the heart of who we are. For the believer, it is an invitation to inner honesty: what is hidden deep within cannot escape God. It also invites sincerity in prayer and repentance.

sens: The attitude of one who believes themselves superior to others
Excessive self-confidence
Refusal to humble oneself or recognize one's limits
Elevation of the heart that turns away from God
H1466.detail: 1. Pride is primarily the attitude of one who stands above others, who believes themselves better or more important: it is a form of heart elevation. In Job 33:17, God wants to keep man from this pride that distances him from Him. 2. It is also excessive self-confidence, the refusal to acknowledge one's weaknesses or needs: one who is filled with pride does not see their need for help. 3. Pride expresses itself in the refusal to humble oneself: in Job 22:29, when humiliation comes (the moment one must bow), the proud man must learn to pray, that is, to recognize his smallness. 4. Finally, it is an elevation of the heart that closes the eyes to God: in Jeremiah 13:17, the pride of the people makes them blind to the coming judgment, and the Prophet weeps over it.
H1466.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising, standing up, elevating oneself. Pride is literally an "elevation" — not physical, but of the heart and self-esteem. This root is found in other Hebrew words designating height or greatness. The image is that of something or someone that stands out, that puts itself forward: it is the opposite attitude of humility, which lowers itself.
H1466.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 33:17, it describes the spiritual trap that God wants to keep man from: the pride that blinds him. In Job 22:29, it is linked to humiliation and the necessity to pray: pride collapses when one recognizes their need. In Jeremiah 13:17, the pride of the people is what makes them deaf to divine warning and hastens their fall into captivity. In all cases, it is an obstacle to the relationship with God, an attitude that closes the heart to His voice.
H1466.portee: Pride is presented throughout Scripture as the enemy of faith. This word reminds us that our first temptation is to believe ourselves self-sufficient, to stand tall instead of humbling ourselves before God. The Bible invites us to recognize our limits and our need: it is in humility and prayer that true relationship with the Lord opens up. To guard against pride is to keep the heart open to God.

sens: Excessive pride, arrogance before God or others
The attitude of one who believes themselves superior and disregards their dependence on God
H1467.detail:
1. Pride is this excessive pride that leads someone to believe they are above others or to forget that they depend on God. It is an attitude of the heart: one values oneself and despises others. In Daniel 4:37, this is precisely what God can lower in one who manifests it — Nebuchadnezzar himself bitterly experienced this before repenting.
2. Fundamentally, pride is a form of spiritual rebellion: one who is afflicted by it refuses their place as a creature submitted to God. They claim an autonomy they do not have and set themselves up as the judge of their own actions, instead of recognizing God's absolute sovereignty.
H1467.origine: This Aramaic word is the exact Aramaic form of the Hebrew word גֵּוָה (ge.vah) which also means "pride" or "excessive pride." Aramaic and Hebrew are sister languages spoken in the ancient Near East; here they share the same root and meaning. This term evokes the idea of self-elevation, a height that one unduly attributes to oneself.
H1467.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, at the heart of Nebuchadnezzar's testimony in Daniel 4:37. The king of Babylon, who experienced divine humiliation — he lost his reason for seven years because of his pride — enumerates here what God has the power to lower us from. It is the wise conclusion of a man who has experienced the fearsome justice of God. The use of the word in this circumstance shows that pride is presented as the sin that most directly attracts divine intervention to bring it down.
H1467.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that pride is incompatible with the fear of God and submission to His sovereignty. Recognizing our limits and our total dependence on God is not weakness, it is wisdom. The account of Nebuchadnezzar invites each one to examine their heart: where do we seek glory? whom do we truly serve?

sens: To move from one place to another, to cross
To disappear, to fade away, to cease to be
(Regarding time, life) To flow quickly
H1468.detail:
1. The word describes the movement of something that crosses space or crosses a boundary. In Numbers 11:31, the wind "blows" from the sea to the camp: it passes from one place to another, bringing the quails. It conveys the idea of movement, of crossing.
2. It also means to disappear or fade away: something that was there is no longer, it goes away. In Psalms 90:10, the pride we derive from our years "passes" quickly: it does not last, it fades away.
3. Applied to time and life, the word expresses the fleeting and ephemeral nature: days flow, pass, and disappear. Our years "pass" like a moment, so brief that we feel like they are flying away (Psalms 90:10).
H1468.origine: The Hebrew verb guz fundamentally evokes the idea of crossing, of traversing a space. The root refers to a movement that passes over or beside something. In the Hebrew Bible, it is used to describe what changes place, goes away, or disappears — whether it is a wind, a cloud, or the course of life. The word belongs to a rich semantic family where passage and crossing are at the heart of its meaning.
H1468.emploi: The verb guz appears only twice in the Bible according to the documented uses. In Numbers 11:31, it designates the wind that blows and crosses space, bringing a material blessing (the quails). In Psalms 90:10, it characterizes the flight of time and human life: the years pass quickly, the pride we derive from them flies away. Both uses share the idea of rapid movement and disappearance — the moving wind, the flowing life. The context of Psalms 90 is particularly rich: it meditates on the brevity of existence in the face of God's eternity.
H1468.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the vanity and fragility of human life. In the face of divine eternity, our days pass like a breath, our pride fades away. It is a call to wisdom: not to cling to the ephemeral, but to seek what endures. At the same time, the passage of the wind bringing the quails (Numbers 11:31) reminds us that God acts through natural phenomena to provide for our needs.

sens: A bird still young, just out of the nest
Figuratively, one who needs protection and nourishment
H1469.detail:
1. The word designates a young bird that has just been born or is still in the nest, dependent on its parents. It is a juvenile bird, not yet an adult. In Genesis 15:9, God asks Abraham to bring a turtle dove and a young pigeon for the sacrifice: these are young birds, considered acceptable for the offering.
2. The image of the young bird is used figuratively to represent someone who needs care and protection. In Deuteronomy 32:11, Moses describes the Lord watching over Israel like an eagle carrying its young on its wings: these young birds symbolize the people of Israel, fragile and dependent on divine providence.
H1469.origine: The Hebrew word gozel comes from a root that describes the action of pecking or feeding. It is formed to designate the chick: one that pecks, that eats, particularly the young birds in the nest that the parents feed. The word evokes the concrete image of a young and hungry creature.
H1469.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 15:9, it qualifies a young pigeon offered in sacrifice — an appropriate victim because it is young and easily accessible. In Deuteronomy 32:11, it appears in a poetic comparison where Moses describes how the Lord educates His people: the eagle fluffs its young, forces them to leave the nest, then catches them on its wings. The word symbolizes the dependent and developing people.
H1469.portee: This image of the young bird reminds the believer of their dependence on God. Just as the chick depends entirely on its parents for food and protection, the people of God — and each believer — depend on divine providence and tenderness. It is an invitation to trust and to recognize that God cares for His children with constant solicitude.

sens: city in Mesopotamia
region of deportation for the Israelites from the Northern Kingdom
river in Mesopotamia
H1470.detail:
1. Gozan is a city in northern Mesopotamia, located on the middle course of the Euphrates. It is always mentioned alongside other places like Chalach, the Chabor, and the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6).
