2. It is the place where the king of Assyria established the exiled Israelites from the Northern Kingdom after the conquest of Samaria in 722 B.C. The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh dwelled there (1 Chronicles 5:26), scattered far from their promised land.
3. In Assyrian political geography, Gozan is among the conquered cities whose gods could not save them, listed alongside Charan and Retseph in the Assyrian challenges to King Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:12).
H1470.origine: The name literally means "a cut" or "a separation." It is both the name of a historical city in Mesopotamia and that of the river that flowed through it. The word may reflect the idea of a rupture, of separation — which takes on symbolic significance for the exiled Israelites, cut off from their homeland.
H1470.emploi: Gozan appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in relation to the exile of the kingdom of Israel by Assyria. It is mentioned twice as a destination for the deportees from Samaria (2 Kings 17:6 and 18:11) and once for the tribes east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:26). It also appears in two parallel accounts where the king of Assyria lists the cities he has conquered to justify his power (2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12). It is primarily a geographical marker of Assyrian captivity.
H1470.portee: Gozan reminds Bible readers of the historical reality of divine judgment on Israel: God's people were scattered far from their land because of their unfaithfulness, forced to live in exile in Mesopotamia. This place symbolizes the rupture, the separation from the divine promise, while remaining a testimony that even in exile, God does not leave His own without a trace in history.

sens: Group of people united by a land, a language, common ancestors
Set of non-Israelite peoples, the foreigners
People of Israel itself considered as a nation
Compact multitude of living beings (figurative sense)
H1471A.detail:
1. A nation is primarily a people living on the same territory with its own language and customs. It is a human group organized around common bonds — land, language, descent. Genesis 10:5 illustrates this well: nations are distinguished by their lands, languages, and families.
2. Very often in the Bible, "nation" refers to peoples who are not Israel, the foreigners or "Gentiles." This meaning arises from the fact that Israel saw itself as a chosen people, separate from others. Deuteronomy 7:1 lists the nations that Moses must fight in Canaan: peoples outside the people of God.
3. Sometimes, the word applies to Israel itself when speaking of its greatness or destiny. God promises Abraham to make him a "great nation" (Genesis 12:2), which shows that Israel is also a nation among others, but with a unique role.
4. In a few passages, the word designates a dense crowd or swarm, like a compact multitude. It is an image of density and collective power.
H1471A.origine: The Hebrew word goy comes from a root that evokes the idea of group or mass. It shares this family with other Hebrew words designating the whole or multiplicity. The word has taken on a particular theological coloring: in the Bible, while Israel is understood as God's chosen people, the goyim (plural) are the peoples who do not know the Lord. This distinction does not disappear but profoundly changes in meaning with the arrival of the Gospel.
H1471A.emploi: The word appears more than 500 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Torah and the prophets. It primarily designates the peoples of the world in their diversity: Genesis 10 lists the nations descended from the sons of Noah, Deuteronomy 7 names the nations that Israel will conquer. At the same time, God promises Abraham that a great nation will arise from him and that through him "all the nations of the earth will be blessed" (Genesis 22:18): Israel itself becomes a nation, but with a mission towards other peoples. The prophets mix the two usages: Isaiah 55:5 says that unknown nations will come to Israel, while Ezekiel speaks of God's name profaned by Israel among the nations where it has been scattered. All this shows a tension: Israel is a nation, but it is also God's instrument to reveal His name to all nations.
H1471A.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the place of Israel and, by extension, the Church. God has not despised the peoples, but He has chosen a people to be the channel of His revelation and blessing to all others. Today, the coming of Jesus expands this meaning: the Gospel is intended for all nations, and the promise made to Abraham is fulfilled when all peoples, without distinction, can access faith in Jesus Christ. The word reminds us that God sees the world as a collection of peoples, and that His plan extends to all.

sens: Kingdom or people of the ancient Near East, ruled by a king
State or region neighboring Israel at the time of the patriarchs and the conquest
H1471B.detail:
1. Gojim designates a small kingdom or state of the ancient Near East, ruled by a king (Tidal according to Genesis 14:1). This name appears as that of a sovereign among other powers of the time: Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar, and Chedorlaomer of Elam. The word evokes an organized political entity, comparable to the neighboring kingdoms of Abraham.
2. At the time of Israel's conquest under Joshua, Gojim is still mentioned as a small kingdom whose king reigns over a territory near Gilgal (Joshua 12:23). It is likely a coastal or mountainous region of the Levant, included in the list of cities conquered by the Israelites.
H1471B.origine: The word גּוֹיִם (goyim) comes from the root גּוֹי (goy), which generally designates a people or a nation. Here, it seems to be used as a proper name of a specific state of the ancient Near East. The same root "goy" is used elsewhere to speak of nations in general, but in these three biblical verses, it functions as the name of a well-defined political entity.
H1471B.emploi: Gojim is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the context of the early Canaanite kingdoms. It first appears in Genesis 14:1-2 and 14:9 as one of the four kings who confront Abraham and his allies to recover prisoners and plunder. Tidal, king of Gojim, is listed alongside three other sovereigns of the ancient Near East. Later, in Joshua 12:23, Gojim reappears in the list of kingdoms defeated by Joshua during the conquest of Canaan, located "near Gilgal." These three usages situate Gojim in the context of Israel's early military conflicts.

sens: Group of people united by a common origin, a common land, a common language, or a common government
Non-Israelite people, foreign to Israel
People of Israel itself
Multitude of animals or insects
H1471G.detail:
1. A nation in the broad sense is a group of people forming a people: they generally share a land, a language, common customs. In Isaiah 66:19, the text speaks of sending messengers "to the nations" — that is, to these different peoples of the known world, Tarshish, Cush, Lud, Tubal, Javan — to announce the glory of God.
2. Very often in the Hebrew Bible, this word specifically designates pagan peoples, that is, all the peoples who do not know the God of Israel and do not worship as Israel does. This is why the Greek of the New Testament often translates this word as "ethnè" (nations, Gentiles).
3. Sometimes the text uses this word for Israel itself, as Israel is also a nation — a nation chosen by God, with its own laws and identity.
4. By figurative extension, the word can designate a multitude of animals or insects acting together, like an army or a swarm, as they form a kind of "people" in motion.
H1471G.origine: The Hebrew word "goy" (גּוֹי) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "rising up" or "being born together" — the image of a group that grows and constitutes itself. The root is also related to "guem" (to emerge), which expresses movement or emergence. The plural of the word, "goyim," designates the nations as a whole. This term is not pejorative in itself; it is simply the Hebrew word for "nation" or "people." In Greek, the New Testament translates it as "ethnos" (ἔθνος), which has given rise to the French word "ethnie."
H1471G.emploi: The word "goy" appears mainly in the prophetic and narrative books of the Old Testament. It primarily designates the peoples foreign to Israel — Egyptians, Philistines, Assyrians, etc. — and then speaks of the "nations" that God must judge or that God uses to chastise His people. But sometimes the text designates Israel itself as a "nation" (as in Exodus 19:6: "You will be for me a kingdom of priests"). In Isaiah 66:19, the eschatological context — the end of times — is striking: God promises that the remnant of Israel will carry His glory "among the nations," that is, to all the peoples of the world, from the most distant to the most forgotten. It is a promise of universality: the knowledge of the God of Israel will not remain confined to Israel.
H1471G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God is not only interested in one people but in all nations. The vision of Isaiah 66:19 announces that the Gospel will be carried to all the peoples of the earth — this is exactly what Jesus commands His disciples in Matthew 28:19-20 ("Make disciples of all nations"). This word invites us to see the world not as a collection of "us" and "them," but as a human family that God loves and for which He wants His name to be known.

sens: a group of people of the same origin, speaking the same language, living under the same government
non-Jewish people, foreign to Israel
H1471H.detail:
1. The word goy refers to an organized human group: a people with its territory, language, and government. In Judges 4:2, Jabin, king of Canaan, reigns over the neighboring nations (peoples), which shows that a goy is a distinct political and social group.
2. In the biblical context, goy often stands in opposition to Israel: it designates the peoples other than the Hebrews. This is the background of the three passages in Judges (4:2, 4:13, 4:16), where Harosheth-Hagoyim, "Harosheth of the nations," is the capital of the Canaanite king Jabin, clearly marking a non-Israelite territory.
H1471H.origine: The word goy comes from a root meaning "to increase, to multiply." A goy is therefore literally a "multitude," a large group. The plural goyim collectively designates all non-Jewish peoples. In Greek, this word was translated as "ethné" (ethnos), from which our French word "ethnie" derives; it reflects the idea of a people united by blood and culture.
H1471H.emploi: The term goy appears 3 times in the provided passages (Judges 4), always in the plural (goyim) and in the proper name "Harosheth-Hagoyim." This place name means "Harosheth of the Nations" and designates the seat of the Canaanite king Jabin. The three occurrences (in verses 2, 13, and 16 of Judges 4) situate the military events around this capital, emphasizing that Jabin reigns over organized and armed peoples. The context shows that goyim applies here to the Canaanite populations, foreign to Israel.
H1471H.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible recognizes the existence and organization of peoples other than Israel. Far from denying them, it situates them within God's plan: the nations have their place, their history, and their responsibility before the Creator. For the Christian reader, this establishes the principle that the Gospel is addressed to all peoples, and that God cares for all nations.

sens: the body of a living person or animal
the corpse, the dead body of a creature
the remains left on a battlefield
the whole body as property, as material possession
H1472.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the physical body of a living being—human or animal—with its flesh and structure. In Genesis 47:18, the Egyptians tell Joseph that they have only their "bodies" (their living persons) and their lands left, showing that the body represents life itself. 2. It also means the corpse, the lifeless body. Judges 14:8-9 speaks of the "body of the dead lion," inside which Samson discovers honey. 3. The word particularly evokes the bodies of warriors fallen in battle. In 1 Samuel 31:10 and 31:12, we read how Saul's corpse is fastened to the walls of Beth-Shan, then torn down and burned—a painful trace of defeat. 4. The body can also represent the whole person, considered as a subject or as property. In Nehemiah 9:37, the Israelites complain that foreign kings dominate over their "bodies," meaning over themselves, over their existence.
H1472.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of the body as a physical unit, distinct from the soul or spirit. In biblical Hebrew, the "body" (geviyyah) often designates the material and visible reality of created life. This term implicitly opposes what is immaterial or spiritual, although Hebrew thought never radically separates the soul from the body.
H1472.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and concrete descriptions. It is found in the accounts of Samson (Judges 14), in the story of Saul (1 Samuel 31), and in the complaints of Israel (Nehemiah 9, Psalms 110). The meaning slightly changes depending on the context: living and active when it comes to servitude or property (Genesis 47, Nehemiah 9), dead and without dignity when it comes to desecrated or mutilated corpses (1 Samuel 31). The word can also appear in heavenly visions to describe the form of superhuman beings (Ezekiel 1, Daniel 10), where it simply means "form" or "visible body."
H1472.portee: This word reminds us that we are embodied beings, that our body is not a prison but a reality that God created and that belongs to us. The Bible does not despise the body: it even respects it after death, as shown by the efforts to honor the remains with dignity. For the Christian, the resurrection of the body taught later in the New Testament is rooted in this biblical esteem for the body as an integral part of our humanity.

sens: State of one who is a prisoner, held away from their country
Group of exiled persons, prisoners of war
Forced deportation of a population
Forced travel, displacement under constraint
H1473.detail:
1. Captivity refers to the state of one who has lost their freedom and is held prisoner, far from their homeland. This is what the Jews experience when Nebuchadnezzar takes them from Jerusalem: "He took all of Jerusalem captive, all the leaders and all the valiant men" (2 Kings 24:14). The word evokes confinement, deprivation of freedom.
2. The term also designates the captives themselves, the community of exiles taken collectively. Ezra speaks of the "sons of the captivity" who celebrate Passover together after their return (Ezra 6:19), thus designating the group of deportees who returned from Babylon.
3. Captivity can also name the act of deportation itself, the moment when an entire population is forcibly taken into exile. It is a national punishment, a brutal rupture with the past.
4. In a more general sense, the word applies to any imposed displacement or forced travel. Ezekiel, to signify the coming exile, acts as a prophet: "I went out by day with my belongings like the belongings of a traveler" (Ezekiel 12:7), using the word to evoke the forced move awaiting Israel.
H1473.origine: The Hebrew word golah comes from a root meaning "to go away, to depart into exile." It paints the image of a forced separation, a tearing away. The word particularly applies to the Babylonian exile (586 BCE), one of the greatest ruptures in Israel's history. The same root produces other words to designate those who depart or are taken away.
H1473.emploi: The word golah appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books after the exile: Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. It primarily designates the fate of the Judeans deported to Babylon in the 6th century BCE (2 Kings 24:14-16). After the return, the exiled returnees call themselves "the sons of the captivity" or "those of the captivity" (Ezra 2:1, 6:19-21), showing that this word profoundly marks their identity. Jeremiah uses it to speak of those who remain (29:16), while Ezekiel sees it from the inside (1:1, 12:7). The word thus designates both the state, the group of people, and the historical event that transformed Israel.
H1473.portee: Exile is a decisive moment in Israel's faith: it is a judgment of God on unfaithfulness, but also a time of purification and renewal. For the Christian, this word reminds us that God may allow trials to correct His people, but He never abandons them. Exile also shows that a nation can rebuild itself after spiritual disaster—a lesson of repentance and hope. For the early readers of the return, this word resonated with their own experience of deliverance.

sens: Fortified city of the tribe of Manasseh, located in Bashan east of the Jordan
H1474.detail: Golan was one of the three cities of refuge established by Moses east of the Jordan, alongside Betser and Ramoth (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). It is a Levitical city assigned to the sons of Gershon, a branch of the Levitical priests, along with its surrounding pasture lands (Joshua 21:27; 1 Chronicles 6:71). It served as a refuge for someone who accidentally or mistakenly killed another, protecting them from the vengeance of the victim's nearest relative.
H1474.origine: The Hebrew name Golan would mean "their captivity" or "their rejoicing" according to ancient etymological traditions, but the exact origin of the word remains uncertain. It is a geographical place name attested in biblical texts to designate this mountainous region of Bashan.
H1474.emploi: Golan appears four times in Scripture. It is mentioned during the designation of the cities of refuge by Moses (Deuteronomy 4:43) and during their official confirmation by Joshua (Joshua 20:8). It also appears in the list of Levitical cities assigned to the family of Gershon (Joshua 21:27; 1 Chronicles 6:71). All uses present it as a city of refuge in Bashan, within the territory of Manasseh.
H1474.portee: The system of cities of refuge, of which Golan was a part, reveals God's mercy towards someone who kills without intent: rather than blind vengeance, the Israelite law offered a protected asylum. It is a powerful example of justice tempered by grace, guiding the believer towards forgiveness and the protection of the innocent.

sens: Hole dug in the ground, deep and dangerous
Trap or hidden danger
Image of misfortune that falls back on the one who prepared it
H1475.detail:
1. A pit is a hole intentionally dug in the ground, deep enough for someone to fall into and get hurt. The text of Ecclesiastes 10:8 illustrates this directly: "He who digs a pit will fall into it."
2. The pit also refers to a trap or danger that one has prepared for oneself. It represents the evil plans one sets against others.
3. Figuratively, the pit evokes the misfortune that falls back on its author: he who digs a trap to ensnare others ends up falling into it himself. It is an image of divine justice that gives to each according to their works.
H1475.origine: The Hebrew word גּוּמָּץ (gummats) comes from a root that means "to dig" or "to make a hole." It designates the concrete result of this action: the dug cavity. This image of the pit is recurrent in biblical Hebrew to speak of traps and dangers, and it often expresses the idea that evil prepares its own downfall.
H1475.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 10:8, where it occupies a key place in the Preacher's teaching. It states a principle of wisdom: he who digs a pit to trap others falls into it himself. This maxim belongs to the genre of wisdom proverbs, where every action has a natural or divine consequence. The pit can be literal (a real hole) or a metaphor for a trap and conspiracy.
H1475.portee: This verse teaches that the evil one prepares for others ultimately reaches oneself. It is a call to prudence and righteousness: in seeking to harm, one destroys oneself. For the Christian, this reinforces the idea that God ensures that justice is fulfilled, and that it is never wise to conspire or prepare misfortune for others.

sens: Son of Naphtali, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
Founder of the family of the Gunites
Descendant of Gad
H1476G.detail:
1. Guni is a son of Naphtali, one of the twelve sons of Jacob who gave rise to the tribes of Israel. He is mentioned among the children of Naphtali with his brothers Jahtzeel, Jetser, and Shillem (Genesis 46:24).
2. Guni is the head of the family from which the family of the Gunites descends, whose name recalls its founding ancestor. This family is counted during the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:48).
3. Guni also appears as a descendant of Gad, showing that this name may have been borne by members of different tribes throughout Israel's history (1 Chronicles 7:13).
H1476G.origine: The name Guni means "my defender" (?) according to ancient sources. It comes from a Hebrew root related to protection or defense. The name is associated with the family of Naphtali, son of Jacob and Bilhah.
H1476G.emploi: Guni is mentioned three times in Scripture, always as a genealogical figure. First in Genesis 46:24, during the list of the sons of Naphtali who went down to Egypt. Then in Numbers 26:48, where he appears as the founder of a clan: from his descendants comes the family of the Gunites, counted during the second census of the Hebrews in the wilderness. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 7:13, he is cited again among the sons of Naphtali. These three mentions show Guni's genealogical importance in the tribe of Naphtali.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad
Father of Abdiel
H1476H.detail: 1. Guni is a man of the tribe of Gad, mentioned only once in the entire Bible, at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. He appears in the genealogy of the heads of families of Gad, indicating that he was an ancestor of significant lineage. 2. He is known as the father of Abdiel, whose son Achi became chief of one of the patriarchal houses of the tribe of Gad (1 Chronicles 5:15). His name founded a family, that of the Gunites, which continued in the life of Israel.
H1476H.origine: The name Guni means "my defender" or "the one who protects me," formed from a root that evokes protection and defense. In Israel, personal names often carry the meaning of a prayer or conviction: this name expresses trust in God as the protector of the family. The name also appears in relation to the tribe of Naphtali (where a Guni is cited as a son of Naphtali and founder of a family), showing that it was a significant name across several generations.
H1476H.emploi: Guni is cited only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:15, in the context of a genealogical list of heads of families of the tribe of Gad at the time of the divided kingdom. He appears in the genealogy as an ancestor of Abdiel and grandfather of Achi, confirming his importance in the clan structure of Gad. This unique mention shows that the biblical text preserves the names of the founding ancestors of the main families of Israel, even when few details are given about their lives.

sens: Family or clan descending from Guni, son of Naphtali
H1477.detail: 1. The Gunites are the members of the clan or family descended from Guni, son of Naphtali. They form one of the families of the tribe of Naphtali, listed during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 26:48). Like all tribal families of Israel, they constitute a group of descendants bearing the name of their ancestor.
H1477.origine: The name comes from Guni, the eponymous father of the clan. Guni was himself one of the sons of Naphtali, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, mentioned as early as Genesis 46:24. The Gunites represent his established descendants during the census in the wilderness, a few generations after the entry into Egypt. The name would mean "my defender" according to some proposals, although this etymology is not certain.
H1477.emploi: The Gunites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:48, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness of Moab, before entering the promised land. They are listed among the families of Naphtali, alongside the Jahtzeelites and other clans. This census marks the fulfillment of God's promise to multiply Abraham's descendants and the organization of the tribes in view of the conquest of Canaan.
H1477.portee: The Gunites remind us that each family, no matter how humble or little mentioned in Scripture, belongs to God's chosen people and participates in the fulfillment of His promises. Even a clan named only once in the Bible is an integral part of the people of Israel, called to receive the promised inheritance.

sens: To breathe one's last, to die
To cease to live, to perish, to be annihilated
To reach the ultimate end of life
To be in agony, to be on the brink of death
H1478.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very physical: it is the moment when the breath of life leaves the body. "Expire" conveys the image of one who exhales their last breath. Ishmael "expired" at one hundred thirty-seven years (Genesis 25:17), simply meaning he ceased to breathe and live.
2. The word more broadly designates death itself, annihilation. All flesh will perish in the flood, for it cannot escape what is coming (Genesis 6:17). This is the inevitable fate.
3. In passages of extreme suffering, the word emphasizes that life is extinguishing. In Numbers 17:12, the people cry, "We are expiring, we are all perishing!": they feel they are dying from fear or hunger.
4. In Job, "expire" can also describe agony, the moment that precedes death. Job wishes he had died from the womb (Job 10:18), and swears he will defend his innocence "until his last breath" (Job 27:5) — the image of breath coming to a halt.
H1478.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּוַע (gava) evokes the panting, the expulsion of vital breath. Its etymology refers to the idea of labored breathing and exhaustion. It is a simple verb, without major derived forms in biblical usage, remaining very concrete: it does not refer to an abstract or poetic death, but to the physical end of a living body.
H1478.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narrative books (Genesis, Numbers) and wisdom literature (Job, Psalms). It regularly describes the natural death of patriarchs: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, all "expire" at the end of long lives. It also names collective destruction: the flood annihilates all flesh (Genesis 6:17 and 7:21), the people perish from hunger and fear in the desert. Job uses it with particular intensity: his words on final agony show him grappling with the question of the meaning of suffering and death. The word remains serious and corporeal: never poetic, never softened.
H1478.portee: This verb brings the reader back to the stark reality of human death — not as an abstract threat or dogma, but as a physical event that everyone will experience. For the believer, it invites reflection on the brevity of earthly life and the vanity of clinging to the present world. The passages of physical death (patriarchs) remind us that life has a limit set by God; the passages of extreme suffering (Job, Psalms) raise the question of what God does with our final moments. It is a word that reorients towards what endures.

sens: To close a door, an entrance, a passage
To prohibit access to a place
H1479.detail:
1. The verb literally means to close a door or a gate to prevent passage. In Nehemiah 7:3, it is the order given to close the gates of Jerusalem by locking them: a concrete and decisive action to secure the city.
2. Figuratively, to close can also mean to block access to something, to prohibit entry — a meaning close to the first, but which emphasizes the idea of blockage and restriction.
H1479.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of closure and sealing. The form used in the Bible (the Hiphil) literally means to make something closed, hence the action of closing a door or an entrance. It is a concrete verb that paints the image of a door being pushed to close it.
H1479.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Nehemiah 7:3. Nehemiah orders the governor and the commander to close the gates of Jerusalem and lock the doors to protect the city. This is in the context of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile, where the security of the walls and gates is crucial. The action of closing is here a military and administrative gesture, entirely material.
H1479.portee: This word reminds us that the protection of a community often involves simple and concrete acts: closing doors, standing guard, organizing security. For the believer, it illustrates how God provides for the protection of His people through ordinary human means, and how vigilance and organization are responsibilities that fall to us.

sens: The physical body of a person, the entirety of their fleshly envelope
The corpse, the mortal remains of a person
By extension, the carcass or remains of one who has ceased to live
H1480.detail:
1. The body is the visible and material physical envelope of a living person, the entirety of their flesh, bones, and limbs. It is the word used when simply referring to the bodily structure.
2. The corpse or remains, it is the body after death, devoid of life. In 1 Chronicles 10:12, the men of Jabesh rise to retrieve the body (corpse) of Saul and those of his sons after their defeat, in order to bury them with dignity.
3. The remains or carcass of a dead creature, all that remains of the body after death. The respect for the dead drives the Israelites to find and honor the remains of their king.
H1480.origine: The Hebrew word גּוּפָה comes from a simple root designating the body as a physical and visible entity. It is a concrete and direct term, without mystical connotation: it simply describes the material body, whether living or dead. The word has no complex etymology; it captures the basic idea of the physical form of a being.
H1480.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 10:12. It designates there the corpse of Saul and those of his sons, fallen in the battle of Mount Gilboa against the Philistines. The context underscores the religious and moral importance of burial: the valiant men of Jabesh risk their lives to retrieve the royal remains and give them an honorable burial, which was a sacred act in Israel. This passage shows that even a king fallen from grace deserves the respect due to his body.
H1480.portee: This word reminds us that the human body, even after death, deserves respect and dignity. For the believer, it is a call to honor the mortal remains, to recognize that the body has value in the eyes of God. The dignified burial of Saul by his subjects remains a testimony of duty towards the dead and of the piety that should transcend political conflicts.

sens: To dwell somewhere temporarily, for a time
To reside as a foreigner, without being a citizen of the place
To stay, to stop in a place
To be established, to have one's dwelling somewhere
H1481A.detail:
1. To dwell somewhere temporarily, for a time: this is the most common meaning of the word. It refers to a stay that is not permanent, a provisional presence. When Abram goes down to Egypt (Genesis 12:10), he comes there to "sojourn" fleeing from famine — it is not his land, and he knows it. The word always evokes the idea of a halt, a passage.
2. To reside as a foreigner, without being a citizen of the place: this refers to a residence without full belonging. The Israelite Law uses this word to refer to the "foreigner who sojourns" among Israel (Leviticus 16:29) — someone who lives there but remains a foreigner. This distinction often appears in the texts of the Law.
3. To stay, to stop in a place: the verb can simply express the fact of being somewhere, without particular emphasis on temporality. When Samson desires to "sojourn forever" in the tent of God (Psalms 61:5), he speaks of a lasting presence, but the verb retains the nuance of one who dwells rather than possesses.
4. To be established, to have one's dwelling somewhere: by extension, the word can refer to a more stable installation, the place where one regularly resides. The old man of Gibeah "sojourned" there (Judges 19:16) — he lived there, it was his home, even though the verb reminds us that he may not have been indigenous.
H1481A.origine: The Hebrew verb גּוּר (gur) expresses the idea of a foreign or temporary presence. Its root is likely related to the idea of "staying close to," of "establishing oneself provisionally." The family of the word includes גֵּר (ger), the noun meaning "foreigner," and גּוּרִים (gourim), "foreigners" — showing that the word carries the image of one who dwells without full belonging. The verb in its reflexive form (hithpolel) can mean "to gather together," as if one were assembling provisionally.
H1481A.emploi: The verb appears 79 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Jeremiah. It is particularly frequent in the Pentateuch, where the Israelite Law regularly uses it to speak of the status of the "sojourning foreigner" (ger) — a central figure of hospitality and law in Israel. The usages show a certain nuance: in the patriarchal narratives (Genesis 12:10, 20:1, 21:34), it expresses forced or circumstantial stays; in the Law, it becomes a technical term to designate a specific social category. In the prophets (Jeremiah 42-44), it can express forced deportation or exile. Psalms 61:5 transforms it into a spiritual image: to dwell in the presence of God.
H1481A.portee: This word reminds the people of God that in this world we are all "sojourners," temporary residents. It establishes the biblical ethic toward the foreigner: since the Israelites themselves "sojourned" in Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:5), they must welcome the foreigner with compassion. For the believer, the term invites one to see oneself as a pilgrim passing through this world, finding one's true dwelling with God alone.

sens: To assemble in secret to do harm
To organize together a plot against someone
To incite rebellion or quarrel
To be ready to harm
H1481B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to assemble, to gather: people who come together, often in secret and with bad intentions. In Psalms 56:7, the enemies "conspire" against the psalmist — they gather secretly to spy, observe his steps, seek to harm him. The image is that of a band organizing.
2. From this comes the idea of preparing together a wicked plot, an ambush. In Isaiah 54:15, God declares that one cannot "form plots" against those He protects — the emphasis is on the planned machination, the concerted evil design.
3. The word can also express agitation, turbulence, a tendency to revolt or quarrel. In Psalms 140:3, those who "meditate on evil plans in their heart" are described as "always ready to make war" — it is a disposition, a permanent posture of combat and trouble.
H1481B.origine: The Hebrew root gur carries the image of movement, agitation, turmoil: something that moves, stirs, rises. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing trouble, turbulence, inner emotion. In biblical Hebrew, this verb can take the simple form (Qal) or reflexive form (Hithpolel: "to excite oneself"), which reinforces the idea of active gathering, mutual excitement.
H1481B.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the psalms and in Isaiah. It is mainly used in contexts of threat against a righteous person: the psalmists David and the Lord speak of those who conspire against them or against the Lord's protected ones. In Psalms 56:7 and 59:4, it is the cry of the psalmist describing the organized hostility of his enemies. In Psalms 140:3, it is a description of the wicked always on alert, ready for battle. In Isaiah 54:15, it is a divine promise: no plot will succeed against the one whom the Lord defends. The word conveys the concerted, collective, and deliberate malice.
H1481B.portee: This word reminds the believer that human malice, even when organized and patient, does not have the final word. The psalms that use it express the confidence that, despite the plots of enemies, the Lord watches over and protects the one who cries out to Him. In Isaiah 54:15, it is a word of consolation: the plans against the people of God will be annihilated. This strengthens those who suffer from the hostility of others.

sens: To be afraid, to tremble before a danger or threat
To respect with fear, to be in awe before someone powerful
To dread the consequences of an action or word
H1481C.detail:
1. To be afraid or tremble in the face of a concrete threat: this is the visceral fear before danger. Moab "was very afraid" at the sight of the army of Israel coming toward him (Numbers 22:3), as one trembles in the face of a threatening reality. It is a physical emotion of fear.
2. To respect or venerate someone powerful with a fear mixed with deference: not daring to resist or disobey them. A judge must "fear no man" because only God renders justice (Deuteronomy 1:17). Saul "was afraid" of David because he saw his power growing constantly (1 Samuel 18:15).
3. To dread the consequences of a reckless word or risky choice: this is the apprehension of future harm. The Lord says: "I fear that their adversaries may misunderstand" the true responsible for His victory (Deuteronomy 32:27). Not to "fear" a false prophet means not to let him intimidate (Deuteronomy 18:22).
H1481C.origine: The Hebrew verb גּוּר (gur) fundamentally expresses the idea of retreating or turning away in the face of something frightening. Fear is primarily a reaction of the body: one retreats, trembles. The word conveys a primary emotion, that which danger or power naturally provokes in one who cannot confront it.
H1481C.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible. It designates several forms of fear: fear before a military threat (Numbers 22:3), awe before divine justice (Psalms 33:8), fear inspired by human authority (1 Samuel 18:15), and fear provoked by a dangerous word or gesture (Deuteronomy 18:22; Deuteronomy 32:27). Unlike other Hebrew words for "to fear" that emphasize religious respect, גּוּר insists on the emotional and often involuntary reaction to what is formidable.
H1481C.portee: This word speaks to the believer about the reality of fear: it is normal and human in the face of threats. But it also teaches that the only one who truly deserves reverential fear is God; to fear a man or his words is to give a creature a power it does not have. For the disciple, it is a call not to let the fear of men paralyze justice or faith.

sens: Young carnivorous animal, particularly the young of a lion or leopard
Young and vulnerable creature, dependent on its mother
Image of emerging strength or ferocity
H1482.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the young of a fierce beast, notably a lion cub or an immature young leopard. It is a young animal that is still nursing or has just been weaned, as illustrated by the image of she-cats nursing their young (Lamentations 4:3: "Even jackals offer the breast; They nurse their young").
2. More broadly, the term evokes vulnerability and dependence: the young one is raised by its mother, protected and fed by her before learning to hunt. In Ezekiel 19, the lioness raises her young and gradually teaches them to tear their prey, transitioning from weakness to predation.
3. In a figurative or metaphorical sense, the word also describes a young strength, a ferocity in development: Judah is compared to a "young lion" in Genesis 49:9, and Dan to a "young lion that leaps" in Deuteronomy 33:22, images of warrior power.
H1482.origine: The Hebrew word גּוּר (gur) belongs to a family of images related to youth and animals. It is related to other terms denoting young age or smallness. The image of the young predator — lion, leopard, or jackal — was very present in the ancient Near East: these creatures embodied the strength, cunning, and agility of young warriors. The root expresses the idea of a young creature already marked by the instinct of the hunter.
H1482.emploi: The word gur appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always to refer to the young of fierce beasts. Genesis 49:9 and Deuteronomy 33:22 use it metaphorically to describe the tribes of Judah and Dan as "young lions," symbols of courage and conquest. Lamentations 4:3 uses it literally: the jackals nurse their young, unlike the mother of Jerusalem who shows cruelty. Ezekiel 19:2-5 makes intense and repeated use of it: the lamentation over the princes of Israel shows them as lion cubs raised for war, gradually learning to devour before being captured. The word remains concrete and vivid: never abstract, it always evokes the vulnerable or conquering youth of predators.
H1482.portee: This word enriches the biblical understanding of the pride and responsibility of God's people. Judah and Dan are "young lions": strong, but also called to grow in obedience to God. In Ezekiel, the lamentation shows how the princes, trained in violence, become prey themselves — a reminder that young strength without wisdom leads to captivity. The image invites the reader to reflect: am I a young and growing creature, learning to live according to God's law, or a young strength given over to its own ferocity?

sens: Place or ascent where King Ahaziah of Judah was struck during his flight
H1483.detail: Gur is a location mentioned only once in the Bible, near Jibleam in Israel. It is the place where King Ahaziah of Judah received a fatal wound while fleeing from King Jehu (2 Kings 9:27). The word likely refers to an ascent or height of land — the Hebrew name evokes the idea of a dwelling or residence — and marks the starting point of the king's agony, which will continue until he reaches Megiddo where he will perish.
H1483.origine: The word gur in Hebrew evokes the idea of staying or dwelling. Here, it designates a locality, probably a recognizable place on the ground, likely named for a characteristic of that site. It is a little-known place name, mentioned only once in the royal annals of Judah and Israel.
H1483.emploi: Gur appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 9:27, during the account of the judgment that God executes against the house of Ahab. King Ahaziah, allied with this wicked regime, is mortally wounded at the ascent of Gur while fleeing Jehu. This specific location is mentioned to inscribe in historical geography the fulfillment of divine judgment: it is precisely there that the king's downfall begins, which will culminate at Megiddo.

sens: Young lion or lion cub
Cry, roar of a young animal
H1484.detail:
1. The word refers to the young lion, the lion cub. In Nahum 2:13, the text shows the lion that "tears for its young," meaning its cubs that it feeds with prey: the image is that of a beast that struggles for its young.
2. The word can also evoke the characteristic cry of these young animals: their roar or distinctive voice. In Jeremiah 51:38, the passage states that the adversaries "will roar like lion cubs," describing the noise made by these fierce young beasts.
H1484.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of crying out or producing a hoarse sound. It primarily designates the young of a carnivorous animal, particularly the lion, and by extension the characteristic cry or roar of this young animal. The family of the word includes other terms related to guttural sounds and young animals.
H1484.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times to refer to lion cubs. In these contexts, it reinforces the image of power and ferocity: the lion protecting its young (Nahum 2:13) or the threatening cries of young animals (Jeremiah 51:38). These passages use the figure of the lion and its offspring to describe formidable realities: destructive strength in Nahum, enemy threat in Jeremiah.
H1484.portee: These two images of lion cubs reveal God's created power in nature, but also His warning: the Bible places them in contexts of judgment or threat, reminding the reader that raw strength and ferocity are realities of the world. The Christian also discovers that God sees and protects His "young ones" (in a figurative sense), just as the lion watches over its cubs.

sens: place inhabited by Arabs, located between Palestine and the Arabian Peninsula
H1485.detail: Gur-Baal is a place whose name literally means "dwelling of Baal" (Baal being a Canaanite deity). It was a region inhabited by Arabs, located in the border area between the lands of Israel and the Arabian desert, probably to the south or southeast of Judah.
H1485.origine: The name consists of two elements: "gur" (dwelling, habitation) and "Baal" (the god Baal worshiped by Canaanite and Levantine peoples). It reflects the religious and geographical environment of the ancient Near East, where place names often associated a geographical term with a local deity.
H1485.emploi: This place appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 26:7, in the context of the military campaigns of King Uzziah of Judah. The text mentions that God helped Uzziah to fight against the Arabs who lived at Gur-Baal, indicating that it was a region of border conflicts between the Israelite kingdoms and the nomadic peoples of the desert.

sens: small object (stone, shard) thrown to make a decision at random
result of the drawing of lots, decision made by lot
portion of territory or property assigned by drawing lots
destiny, what is allotted to someone by chance or Providence
H1486.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the material objects that were thrown to decide: small stones or marked shards of pottery, cast like dice. When Leviticus speaks of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:8), Aaron "shall cast lots for the two goats" to designate which will be offered to the Lord and which will bear the sins of the people.
2. The act of drawing lots itself, and its result: the word denotes the action of "casting lots" and the decision that follows. Proverbs 18:18 states: "The lot puts an end to disputes and decides between the mighty" — it is the drawing that resolves disputes by ending debates.
3. The portion, the domain assigned by drawing lots. This is the dominant meaning in Joshua: each tribe of Israel receives "its allotted share by lot" (Joshua 16:1), a specific territory. The Levites also cast lots to determine which cities will belong to them (1 Chronicles 6:54).
4. In a figurative sense, it refers to destiny, what is allotted to someone. Psalm 16:5 says: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my lot" — no longer a geographical region, but the personal destiny that the believer entrusts to God.
H1486.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to divide" or "to share." It has given rise in Hebrew to several words in the same family expressing the idea of sharing and portion. Drawing lots was a common practice in antiquity for making decisions: instead of disputing or negotiating, one left the decision to chance, which many considered an expression of divine will. This is why the lot was a legitimate and respected means in the civil, military, and religious life of Israel.
H1486.emploi: The word appears 67 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books. It is very frequent in Joshua (about 25 occurrences) as the entire book recounts the division of the Promised Land among the twelve tribes by drawing lots: "The lot allotted to the sons of Joseph" (Joshua 16:1). It is also found in Chronicles for the lots that assigned the duties of the priests and Levites (1 Chronicles 24:5; 26:13). The book of Esther uses it for the sinister lot that Haman casts to determine the date of the massacre of the Jews (Esther 3:7). In the Psalms and Proverbs, the word rises to a more spiritual meaning: the lot becomes the destiny entrusted to God. Throughout these uses, the fundamental meaning remains: a portion determined by a decision that escapes human choice.
H1486.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that life is not entirely under their control. Casting lots was to entrust an important decision to God, acknowledging that He alone knows the future and governs all things. For Israel, the division of the land by lot meant that each tribe received exactly what God intended for them. Today, this word reminds the reader that behind the appearances of chance operates a divine wisdom and will: our destiny, our gifts, our responsibilities are assigned to us by the One who "governs all things." It is a call to accept one's portion with gratitude and to see God's hand even in what seems random.

sens: Hardened and compact mass of earth
Crust of dried earth or mud on the surface of the ground
Crust or dried deposit on the skin
H1487.detail: 1. The word refers to a solid, hardened, compact mass of earth or earthly material — what forms on the surface when the earth dries and becomes rigid. This is the concrete image of the word: the earth hardening. 2. Specifically, a crust of earth or mud that dries and forms a shell on the surface. This crust can crack and split. 3. In Job 7:5, the word is used figuratively to describe the disgusting deposits and crusts that cover the skin of the sick: it refers to a "earthy crust" that gives the skin the appearance of dry and cracked earth, a visible sign of suffering and the decay of the body.
H1487.origine: The Hebrew word gush comes from a root that expresses the idea of rain, watering, or moisture that recedes — hence the image of what has been wet and then hardened as it dries. This is why the word primarily evokes a crust of earth: from soil soaked with water that has dried and formed a rigid crust. The image of hardness and dryness is central.
H1487.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 7:5. In this context, Job describes his body ravaged by illness: his worms and his skin covered with an earthy crust — an image of living decomposition and extreme physical decay. The usage is deliberately repugnant: Job paints himself as a living corpse. The word takes on poetic force by associating dry and hardened earth with the suffering of a decaying body.
H1487.portee: This word reminds the reader of the real weight of physical suffering described in the Bible, far from any sentimentality. Job does not say he is suffering — he shows his body ravaged, covered in crusts, a stark image of abandonment and misfortune. This teaches the Christian that God also hears the cry of the suffering body, and that describing one's pain honestly is a form of prayer that is heard.

sens: The wool cut from a sheep or goat
The product of shearing, what has been shaved off
The mown grass or regrowth in a field
H1488.detail: 1. The fleece is the wool that is cut from sheep and goats during shearing. In Deuteronomy 18:4, it is listed among the first fruits (the first products) that the owner must give to the priest, like wheat and oil: it is a valuable asset of livestock. 2. The word also refers to the concrete result of the action of shearing or cutting: what has been removed by shearing. In Job 31:20, Job says he has warmed the poor with the fleece of his lambs, meaning with the wool he has sheared. 3. By extension, the word applies to the mown grass of a field. In Psalms 72:6, rain falls on a mown field (literally "field of fleece"), and in Amos 7:1, the regrowth comes after the king's cutting, showing that the harvest leaves a regrowth.
H1488.origine: The Hebrew word gez comes from a root meaning "to cut, to shear." It denotes the product of an action of cutting: first the sheared wool of sheep, then by analogy the mown grass or plants. The common image is that of what has been removed by a blade or shearing.
H1488.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible. In Deuteronomy 18:4, it refers to a legal obligation: the fleece of the sheep is a share that the owner must give to the priests. In Job 31:20, it is a sign of generosity and solidarity towards the poor. In Psalms 72:6 and Amos 7:1, the word shifts towards an agricultural meaning: it denotes not the wool, but the grass of the field, either the mown land or the regrowth that sprouts after the royal harvest. This extension from the concrete (sheared wool) to the abstract (harvested field) follows the logic of the verb "to cut."
H1488.portee: The fleece reminds the reader of the importance of sharing the fruits of one's labor with those who serve God and with the poor. It is also a concrete symbol of divine provision: the wool clothes and warms. Finally, it evokes the cycle of nature and harvest, where even after the cutting, creation resumes and produces regrowth.

sens: One who manages the money and property of a king or institution
High-ranking officer responsible for the public treasury
H1489.detail:
1. The treasurer is the trusted man responsible for keeping, counting, and distributing the money and valuable goods of the sovereign. It is a position of honor and responsibility. In Ezra 1:8, Mithredath the treasurer of King Cyrus hands over the sacred vessels of the temple of Jerusalem that the king has released to Sheshbazzar: it shows that only a trusted officer could handle these important treasures.
2. The term also more broadly designates a high administrative officer, a member of the royal court, with responsibilities over the entire wealth of the kingdom.
H1489.origine: The Hebrew word גִּזְבָּר is of Persian origin (ganzabara), borrowed from the language of the Achaemenid Empire. It entered Hebrew during contact with Persia, particularly during the time of exile and return. This borrowing reflects the historical context: under the reign of the Persian king Cyrus, the treasurer involved is an officer of the Persian government.
H1489.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 1:8. It specifically refers to Mithredath, the treasurer of King Cyrus of Persia, at the time when Cyrus allows the Judeans to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. Mithredath is given the mission by the king to return all the sacred vessels stolen by Nebuchadnezzar and to entrust them to Sheshbazzar, governor of Judah. It is a crucial administrative role in the drama of the return from exile.
H1489.portee: This passage shows how God even uses pagan authorities to accomplish His purposes. The treasurer of the Persian king becomes the instrument through which the treasures of the temple return to Judah. It teaches the reader that God reigns over all kingdoms and can touch the hearts of kings to free His people and restore His worship.

sens: Officer responsible for managing the money and property of a king or administration
H1490.detail: 1. Treasurer: an official responsible for financial management in the service of a royal or governmental authority. The word designates one who keeps, counts, and distributes resources according to orders. In Ezra 7:21, King Artaxerxes orders the treasurers of his province to provide Ezra with everything he requests for the temple of God.
H1490.origine: The word גִּזְבָּר (gizbar) comes from Aramaic, the language spoken in the Persian Empire. It designates an administrative agent in charge of the treasury. It is a technical term from the Persian government, borrowed from the bureaucratic system of the time. It corresponds to the meaning of the Hebrew word of the same root (H1489), both reflecting the institutions of the empire that dominated the world at the time of Ezra.
H1490.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Ezra 7:21. It refers to the Persian officials in charge of the treasury in the provinces of the empire. The context shows that these officers had to obey the king's orders and make available the requested resources. It is an administrative term that reflects the bureaucratic organization of the Persian Empire in the 5th century B.C.
H1490.portee: This word illustrates how God used the structures of secular power — even that of a pagan king — to accomplish His plans for His people. The Persian treasurers, unknowingly, contributed to the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem by obeying the orders of King Artaxerxes inspired by God.

sens: to slice, divide by cutting
to remove by cutting
to separate, detach
H1491.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of slicing or dividing something by passing a sharp instrument through it. It is the concrete gesture of a knife, axe, or razor that separates the parts of an object. In Psalms 71:6, the psalmist speaks of the one who "cut" him from his mother's womb at the moment of birth — an image of the natural separation of the child from his mother.
2. The word also designates the action of removing a part by slicing: to withdraw, amputate, detach. It conveys the idea of cutting off, depriving something that was part of the whole.
3. Figuratively, "to cut" can express a separation, a rupture, a division between things or states — like the transition from maternal life to autonomy.
H1491.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that paints the image of sharpness, of a knife, of what divides. The form here is a participle (the one who cuts, the one who has cut), expressing not a punctual action but a state or quality. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew where the movement of cutting, of separation is central.
H1491.emploi: The verb gazah appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 71:6. It is a hapax — a unique word — which makes its use all the more remarkable. The psalmist, aged and reflecting on his life, addresses his prayer to God by recalling how God "cut him from the womb" of his mother. The image is that of natural birth, the moment when the umbilical cord is cut and the child becomes independent. Thus, it is a verb of separation, linked to life and existence from the beginning.
H1491.portee: This word reminds us that our existence begins with a cut, a separation — that of our birth. The psalmist cites it to say that it is God who has guided his life from that first moment. He invites the reader to see in God the protector who has preserved his life from the moment he was separated from his mother's womb. This image of the original cut becomes the foundation of trust in divine providence: if God made me born and entrusted me to Him from that critical moment, He will continue to keep me.

sens: Thick wool covering a sheep or lamb
Figuratively: the product or sign received from an action or prayer
H1492.detail:
1. The fleece is the thick wool that grows on the skin of sheep and lambs. It is a simple and concrete word: Gideon places a fleece of wool in the threshing floor to see if it will be covered with dew (Judges 6:37).
2. The fleece can also refer to a sign, a product obtained from something. For Gideon, it becomes the means by which he asks God for proof — a "fleece" to test His will: he squeezes the fleece to extract the water that has condensed on it (Judges 6:38), and then he reverses the test (Judges 6:39-40). The word then takes on the meaning of the result, of what is received as confirmation.
H1492.origine: The Hebrew word gazzah comes from a root that means "to shear" or "to cut." The fleece is therefore the wool that has been cut or sheared from the sheep. It is a concrete term from the pastoral world, familiar to all Israelite shepherds.
H1492.emploi: The word appears only in the account of Gideon (Judges 6:37-40), exactly four times. Gideon asks God for a sign to confirm that he must deliver Israel: he places his fleece in the threshing floor. The first night, the fleece is covered with dew while the rest of the ground remains dry (Judges 6:37-38). Gideon, cautious, asks for an inverse sign: that the fleece remain dry and that the ground be covered with dew (Judges 6:39-40), and God does it. The fleece thus becomes the symbol of a request for confirmation, a "fleece test" as it is still called today.
H1492.portee: The account of Gideon and his fleece teaches that seeking a sign from God is human and sometimes legitimate, especially when one doubts their calling. However, it also shows that God can respond to our requests for confirmation. This passage remains a source of inspiration for believers who, like Gideon, ask God for signs to know His will in important decisions.

sens: inhabitant or descendant of Guizon
H1493.detail: 1. Guizon refers to a man from Guizon, a locality about which nothing else is known. Jonathan, son of Shage, is identified as Guizon in the list of David's warriors — indicating that this nickname comes from the place he was from.
H1493.origine: The name Guizon is a Hebrew gentilice (a term that denotes a person's geographical or familial origin). It likely derives from a place named Guizon, but this place is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The formation of this type of name — adding a suffix to a geographical name — is common in Hebrew to indicate belonging or origin.
H1493.emploi: Guizon appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:34. It is a patronymic or gentilice in a list of David's mightiest warriors. Jonathan, son of Shage, is identified there as Guizon. This unique mention does not allow us to understand exactly where Guizon was located or what its significance was, but it confirms that it was a region or family well-known enough to serve as identification.

sens: To cut the wool or hair of an animal
To cut, shave the hair or beard
To harvest, reap
To be destroyed, to disappear
H1494.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: to cut the fleece of sheep or goats to harvest their wool. This is a regular agricultural practice in Israel. Laban goes to "shear his sheep" (Genesis 31:19), and David has "shearers" who work at the annual shearing (1 Samuel 25:2), an important time of the year for shepherds when they gather the flocks.
2. By extension, to shave the hair or beard of a person, an act that often expresses mourning or humiliation. Job, struck by misfortune, "shaved his head" as a sign of distress (Job 1:20). It is a dramatic act that accompanies suffering.
3. In a broader agricultural sense, to harvest or reap, meaning to cut the grains. The idea of quick and systematic cutting also applies to the harvesting of crops.
4. In the passive voice, to be cut, annihilated, to disappear: the prophetic threat "you will be shaved" means that you will be destroyed or humiliated (Jeremiah 7:29, Micah 1:16).
H1494.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the action of cutting, trimming. The basic image is that of the scissor or sickle action that removes, takes away. Related words exist in other Semitic languages with the same meaning of cutting or trimming. The word paints the violent and rapid act of separating the wool from the animal's body, or the hair from the head.
H1494.emploi: The verb appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mostly used in a pastoral context: the shearing of sheep is a well-known, festive, and important operation for the rural economy (Genesis 31:19, Genesis 38:13, 1 Samuel 25:2-7, 2 Samuel 13:23). We also see the act of shaving the head or beard as a sign of misfortune or humiliation (Job 1:20). Later, the prophet Isaiah uses it to describe the silent Servant, "shorn" like a lamb (Isaiah 53:7), and the prophets of judgment use it to announce destruction: shaving then signifies that one has lost dignity and protection (Jeremiah 7:29, Micah 1:16, Nahum 1:12).
H1494.portee: This word reminds us that God knows the everyday actions of men—even the humblest, like the shearing of flocks. It also emphasizes how the human body and its appearances can express moral distress: shaving the hair reflects the inner suffering. Finally, its prophetic use warns that the destruction of the people is never far away when they stray from God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of Egypt and the desert
Son of Caleb and Ephah
H1495G.detail: Gazez is a character from the Old Testament, a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is a son of Caleb, born to his concubine Ephah (1 Chronicles 2:46). The text also mentions a second Gazez, son of Haran, who was himself a son of Caleb and Ephah: this second Gazez is born to Haran according to 1 Chronicles 2:46.
H1495G.origine: The name Gazez means "one who shears" or "the shearer," derived from the Hebrew root גָּזַז which means "to shear" or "to shave." This root evokes the image of one who cuts the fleece of sheep, a common activity among the shepherds of the people of Israel. The name likely describes a function or characteristic related to livestock raising.
H1495G.emploi: Gazez appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:46, in the genealogy of Caleb. The text presents him as the son of Ephah, Caleb's concubine, and mentions that Haran fathered Gazez. This genealogical passage in 1 Chronicles 2 is important because it lists the descendants of Caleb, one of the great patriarchs of Judah, and shows how families developed through the generations.

sens: son of Haran, himself son of Caleb
H1495H.detail: Gazez is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the genealogy of Caleb. He is the son of Haran, who was himself the son of Caleb and his concubine Ephah (1 Chronicles 2:46). His name means "shearer" or "one who shears," possibly referring to a profession or a family characteristic related to livestock raising.
H1495H.origine: The name Gazez comes from a Hebrew root that means "to shear" or "to shave," likely in reference to the shearing of sheep. It is a common descriptive name in ancient genealogies, where names often reflected an activity or remarkable quality of the bearer.
H1495H.emploi: Gazez is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:46, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Judah and more specifically of Caleb. He appears in the context of enumerating the sons and grandsons of Caleb from his concubine Ephah. This passage shows the importance that the Bible places on recording genealogies, even for children born from less official relationships.

sens: stone that has been cut, shaped, and fashioned according to a plan
stone extracted and worked for construction
the work of sculpting or shaping stone
H1496.detail:
1. A cut stone is a stone that has been cut and shaped to give it a regular and precise form. The Hebrew word גָּזִית comes from the verb "gazaz," which means to cut, to shape: it thus designates the result of this action. In Exodus 20:25, God forbids Moses from building the altar with cut stones, because the chisel — the tool — could profane the altar. This prohibition reveals that shaping the stone modifies what God has created.
2. In the accounts of the construction of the temple and the royal palace (1 Kings 5-7), cut stone becomes a noble material, reserved for great works: Solomon has "magnificent cut stones for the foundations" extracted (1 Kings 5:17), and the text emphasizes the meticulous work: they are "cut according to measurements, sawed with the saw, inside and outside" (1 Kings 7:9). The cut stone symbolizes excellence and solidity here.
3. The term can also evoke the very act of cutting, the work of chiseling and squaring that this material requires.
H1496.origine: The Hebrew word גָּזִית derives from the verb גָּזַז (gazaz, "to cut, to shape"). The root expresses the action of slicing, shaping by means of tool strikes. It also appears in other contexts of cutting: shearing flocks, for example. In biblical Hebrew, this family of words always designates a work of separation or division by force, hence the very material and concrete meaning of "cut stone, shaped stone."
H1496.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in relation to monumental construction. It is used mainly in the accounts of the Jerusalem temple and Solomon's palace (1 Kings 5-7 and 1 Chronicles 22). In Exodus 20:25, it refers to the stones that must *not* be cut for the desert altar — a striking contrast. Later, Isaiah 9:9 and Amos 5:11 mention cut stones in relation to the prosperity of kingdoms, while Lamentations 3:9 and Ezekiel 40:42 associate them with the great structures of the sanctuary. The word is thus anchored in the architectural and symbolic context of power, order, and solidity.
H1496.portee: Cut stone speaks to us of the difference between what is worked by man and what is in its natural state. In Exodus 20:25, the prohibition of cut stones for the altar teaches that sincere worship does not need human "finishing" — God prefers simplicity. Conversely, the temple built by Solomon with magnificent cut stones shows that the excellence of work can also glorify God when undertaken according to His will. This word invites us to reflect on the place of our effort, technique, and art in the service of God.

sens: to take something by force from someone, without right or permission
to seize goods or land by violating the rights of the owner
to remove violently, to snatch away
to deprive someone of what belongs to them, to oppress them economically
H1497.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is to seize or remove something by force. In Genesis 21:25, Abraham reproaches Abimelech that his servants have "seized" a water well by force: they have taken by violence what did not belong to them.
2. This verb also designates armed robbery, the act of a bandit who strips the traveler. Proverbs 22:22 warns: "Do not rob the poor," meaning do not steal from him, do not mistreat him to take his goods.
3. To steal sometimes means to take property or land in a violent and unjust manner. Micah 2:2 denounces those who "covet fields and seize them," who take the lands of others by force.
4. The word is also used figuratively to describe economic oppression: one who steals from the poor, who takes away the fruit of their labor or their means of living. Ezekiel 18:18 reproaches one who "has committed robbery" against others, who has plundered them of their goods.
H1497.origine: The verb gazal comes from a root that evokes the idea of seizing, snatching, taking violently. It describes the brutal action of one who takes something from another without permission. The word is used in the context of biblical law of restitution: in Leviticus 5:23, one who has stolen something must return it and add a fifth. The root speaks of the act of unjust dispossession, very different from voluntary giving or fair exchange.
H1497.emploi: The verb appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah). It primarily designates simple theft: Psalms 69:5 states, "What I did not steal, I must restore." But it also extends to violent robbery (Judges 9:25, where the robbers "plunder" the passersby) and especially to the economic oppression of the poor. The prophets use this word to denounce social injustices: Jeremiah 21:12 and 22:3 command to "deliver the oppressed" from the one who plunders them. Ezekiel repeatedly returns to one who "snatches" the goods of others as a grave sin. The word thus expresses both the crime of the robber and the sin of the rich who dispossess the weak.
H1497.portee: This verb reveals that God considers theft and economic oppression as serious sins: the Bible forbids taking by force what belongs to another, and it particularly defends the poor against those who plunder them. For the Christian, it is a call to justice: to respect the property of others, not to exploit the weak, and to restore what has been taken unjustly. It is also a warning: God does not remain indifferent to economic oppression and violence against the poor.

sens: theft or taking of another's property by fraud or violence
goods taken by force or stolen from someone
act of oppression or injustice against the weak
dishonest accumulation of wealth
H1498.detail:
1. Robbery is primarily a concrete act: taking what belongs to another, either by deceit (by stealth) or by force. In Leviticus 5:21, it is listed alongside theft and unreturned deposits — clear violations of another's property rights.
2. It also designates the object of theft: the goods themselves that have been taken. Psalm 62:11 warns: "Do not put your vain hope in robbery," speaking of wealth obtained through theft.
3. Robbery takes on a moral and social dimension: it becomes synonymous with oppression of the weak. Ezekiel 22:29 describes a people who "commit robbery, oppress the unfortunate and the needy," showing that it is a system of injustice.
4. More broadly, it represents the deliberate accumulation of wealth by dishonest and selfish means. Isaiah 61:8 directly opposes it to the justice that God loves.
H1498.origine: The Hebrew word gazal (גָּזַל) comes from a root that literally means "to snatch" or "to take by force." It describes the brutal or cunning action of taking something from someone. Related to gezel (גֵּזֶל, "violence"), it belongs to a family of words that all express unjust appropriation and violation of another's rights. The root emphasizes the active and voluntary nature of theft: it is not a loss, but an act committed against someone.
H1498.emploi: The word robbery appears 6 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Ezekiel) and the wisdom books (Psalms, Ecclesiastes). In Leviticus, it is listed among legal violations that require restitution. In the prophets, it becomes a symptom of an unjust society: Ezekiel denounces it among the princes and the people as a sign of divine judgment (18:18, 22:29). Isaiah opposes it to the justice that God cherishes and promises to punish (61:8). In the Psalms and Ecclesiastes, it symbolizes ill-gotten wealth, deceptive and without lasting value.
H1498.portee: Robbery highlights that stealing or oppressing is never hidden from God's eyes: He hates injustice, especially that which strikes the weak. For the believer, this word reminds us that wealth obtained through fraud or violence has no solid foundation and attracts God's judgment. It also invites honesty in business and respect for the rights of others, especially the most vulnerable.
